Heading: Film review - Indian Express
Content:
The reflection of the recession in the economy can be seen in the city markets as shopkeepers report relatively low footfalls in the festive season

With the stock market dipping down, this year Diwali does not seem to have brought the usual smile to the shopkeepers in the city. Although being the season that brings a boom in most businesses, retailers feel that this Diwali the brunt of economic recession has hampered their sales to quite an extent.

"Diwali is the peak time for the sales of garments, clothing, electronic goods and even precious metal, and even an average buyer adds this expenditure to his budget. But this year, the sale suggests that the business is going through a bad phase in every market," says Bharat Ranka, of National Fabrics on M G Road. "Even though people are buying new clothes, the business has slid down heavily. It is almost 40 per cent less compared to the sales of last year," he says.

"The boom of festive season seems to have slacked as sales are just like any other ordinary day," says Smita, owner of an artifacts shop in Camp, who blames the slump in economy for the depletion of business in the various stores. "We feel that it's the recession in overall economy that has affected the purchasing power of the people which in turn has affected business everywhere," she adds. "In comparison to the number of buyers that we had last year, this time we have less footfalls. Sales are not very good during Diwali season," says Feroz Sheikh, sales manager, Hiroli's Nazakat and Larry Aanandani of Royal Lady garments in Clover Centre.

The scene is similar in the shops of the otherwise busy Laxmi Road, which is the shopping destination of middle-class and upper-middle class buyers. "Recession is not only in the share market but it's the overall economy that has depleted. Sales are not as how we had experienced last year," says Amol Pethekar of Prakash Departmental Stores. But some shops seem to do fairly well. "The boom period of Diwali may not be there but there are sufficient sales, better than ordinary days. We are expecting better sales till Sunday," says manager of Family Shoppee on Kunte Chowk.

Heading: Stuck home, with a PG degree to wield - Indian Express
Content:
Oh so cool
Movie: Roadside Romeo
Voice cast: Saif Ali Khan, Kareena Kapoor, Jaaved Jaaferi
Directed by: Jugal Hansraj
Showing at: Inox, E-square, Citypride, Adlabs
INDIAN animation has finally come of age. Roadside Romeo, the first Walt Disney-Yash Raj roll-out is a barrel of fun: bole toh, ekdum jhakaas, baap.
It combines the best aspects of both studios—Disney's expertise in creating animated figures which live and breathe, and Yash Raj's forte in frothy romance.
Romeo is a one-time pampered pooch, now abandoned on the mean streets of Mumbai. Laila is a saucy, dancer. Trouble looms in the shape of the pug-ugly Charlie Anna (Jaaved Jaaferi). The alacrity with which the characters break into song-and-dance shows that Disney or no Disney, Bollywood rules. Whether style-bhai Romeo is kicking up his heels with his canine pals, or looking for a likely spot to pee ("Yahaan koi toilet nahin hai kya? Man, what a dump") you can actually see Saif, who does cool like no else. And when sexy Laila shakes her charming rump, breathily coming on to her besotted beau, you know that's Kareena. Both sizzle up the screen.
Where debutant director Jugal Hansraj falters is with the villainous Chaaaarrrlie Anna: Jaaferi is made to growl incomprehensibly and break wind more often than getting a chance at being a riot. He does make you guffaw, but only once in a while, and for someone of Jaaferi's goofy brilliance, that's not enough.
But we can live with this Charlie. Roadside Romeo is Hindi cinema's first stylish, slick animated feature, which pulls off the toughest feat - appealing to both adults and children.
That's, like, cool, dude.

Lost glory
Film: Heroes
Cast: Salman Khan,Sunny Deol,Bobby Deol,Mithun Chakraborty,Preity Zinta
Director: Sameer Karnik
Running at: Inox, E-square, Citypride, Adlabs
TWO city slickers set out to deliver letters from dead servicemen to their far-flung families, and in the process, discover themselves.
The premise of Heroes is interesting. And in parts Samir Karnik's film does manage to say what it set out to: That pride (the Hindi garv is a better word) keeps the families of the deceased soldiers going, that we civilians sleep peacefully only because someone has given up their life for us, and that we have a country only because we have a brave fauji guarding our borders. But the director wrings tears out of so many situations that everything turns trite.
Heroes needed a radical change in treatment, but falls half-way between keeping things low-key, and going full-tilt at melodrama. What can you do if pretty Preity Zinta is a war-widow, speaking flawless Punjabi, keeping it together for her old in-laws, and a young son? And Salman Khan, her bluff Jat heartthrob, who says: Teri liye lakh jawani, par yeh jawani desh ke naam, or words to that effect. Sunny Deol plays a rum-swilling disabled airman who loses younger brother Bobby Deol, who carried a torch for the Army. Mithun Chakraborty is an embittered father, who hasn't forgiven son Dino Morea for dying. And the two boysarmed with a camera and alarming naivete, are Sohail Khan and Vatsal Sheth.
This subject deserved a better film.

Heading: Probe on land deals: Medha in race with government panel - Indian Express
Content:
62% women with masters degree homemakers: study

In their late 20s and armed with masters degrees, they are now tied to home, doing daily chores. This is what an overwhelming 62.65 per cent of women who have completed their graduation doing, according to a study.

Incidentally, this percentage is the highest as compared to other categories — illiterate women, women who have completed matriculation or hold a technical diploma or certificate.

This data has been studied in detail by a woman, Sangeeta Upadhyay.

Upadhyay, a professor with Gokhale Institute of Politics and Economics (GIPE) has brought it out in her working paper titled 'Economics of Higher education with special reference to women'.

According to Upadhyay, an analysis of the 1991 and 2001 census data reflects that although the percentage has reduced from 70.57 per cent in 1991, the percentage is the highest among all the other qualification groups.

For instance, "only 32.67 per cent of illiterate women were tied to household chores, as compared to 51.31 per cent women who completed matriculation or secondary education and 35.32 per cent holding a technical diploma," she cites in the paper.

Upadhyay cites various reasons for this trend, one being unemployment. Unemployment among the graduates-and-above category in 2004-2005 was 36.3 per cent for urban women, while it was 30.4 per cent in rural areas, she said. Secondly, the income of a postgraduate woman at a particular position in many an industry is lower than her male counterpart. "For instance, according to the National Sample Survey Organisation (NSSO), the average salary per day received by a graduate-and-above urban female working in a non-agricultural sector is Rs 269.29 per day, while that of her male counterpart is Rs 366.76 per day," she states.

Upadhyay added that returns from education are popularly measured according to income. "However, considering this trend, parents will stop spending on their daughters' postgraduate education, if they end up doing household chores," she said.

Speaking on the trend, Vidyut Bhagwat, director of Krantojyoti Savitribai Phule Women's Study Centre, University of Pune, said there was nothing surprising in the findings.

"Irrespective of the woman's qualification, whether she should work or not depends on the family she is married into. Broadly, a qualified woman is not allowed to work because the family is financially sound or the family disapproves of her job for various reasons," she said.

Heading: Diwali tool to catch voter attention - Indian Express
Content:
Social activist Medha Patkar is now hot on the trail of a committee set up by the state to probe into land deals in Maval and Muslhi Talukas in Pune district. She has set up her own committee to conduct a parallel probe.

State Rehabilitation Minister Patangrao Kadam had announced the committee earlier this month to probe into the land issues.

Both committees have set a two-month deadline for getting their respective reports ready.

"The government has announced a committee, but we felt a parallel one was needed to look into this long-pending issue," Patkar told The Indian Express.

Patkar, batting for 5,000-odd families affected by various projects in the area, had recently taken out a rally and staged a fast to put pressure on the government over the matter. The projects inlcude the Tata Power Project, Pawna dam, Lavasa Lake City and Sahara City. The state committee is to be headed by Additional Chief Secretary Neela Satyanarayan and has two other members, Secretary, Rehabilitation, Ramesh Kumar and Revenue Secretary J P Dange, on the panel. It will seek reports from Pune Collector Chandrakant Dalvi and Divisional Commissioner Nitin Kareer.

Patkar's committee, on the other hand, has Bombay High Court advocate Y P Singh, anti-corruption activist Arvind Kejriwal, former Inspector General of Police S M Mushrif and senior advocate from Dhule, Nirmal Suryavanshi.

The state's inquiry panel is ready to start its work.

The DC will hear the complaints shortly. "We have a list of affected people from the backward community and will also check the issue of ownership of land in these areas," said DC Kareer.

Meanwhile, Patkar, who had earlier demanded a CBI inquiry into the deals, said the parallel committee will study data and documents from official sources, affected people and non-governmental agencies. "We will visit the affected areas and hold public hearings, besides dialogue with officials and other parties," said Patkar.

The inquiry committee will be looking into complaints of land acquisition, compensation and the lease deals related to the Tata Power Project (Siravta, Somwadi, Valvan, Bhushi, Thokalewadi and Mulshi areas), the Pawna, Kasasai, Malwani, Andhre, Jadhavwadi and other dams, besides the Lavasa City and Sahara City projects. Extra land acquired but not used for the projects woul be looked into and any illegalities involved in transfer of land acquired from the affected families would be assessed, said Patkar.

Patkar's panel will also study the use of water and water bodies of these dams, their planned and attained use and the resultant violation of any rights of the dam-project-affected and suggest appropriate ways to use the water for the benfit of the affected people.

Heading: Move to cut HIV patients’ travel to city - Indian Express
Content:
125 events lined up in 5 days, most of them sponsored directly or indirectly by leaders of political parties

Ahead of elections, leaders of political parties have got a handy tool to bedazzle voters. The cultural tool being used are over cultural programmes during Diwali and 125 are lined in five days of next week. Political leaders are directly or indirectly sponsoring most of them.

Around 15 years back, some cultural organisations started 'Diwali Pahat' programmes in the city. They are held early in the morning and include music, celebrity interviews, poetry and dance. Over the years, they have started drawing huge crowds and now political leaders are trying to cash in.

"The programmes are held at every nook and corner besides major auditoriums," said Mohan Kulkarni, well-known event manager in the city. "Sitting and former corporators, MLAs and political wannabes are also directly or indirectly arranging the programmes," he said.

"Sponsorship is the easiest way to reach their audience. Some use their names on tickets, give greeting cards to the audience and felicitate senior citizens or achievers in their constituencies," said Kulkarni.

Suneel Mahajan, one of the event managers, who started the concept of Diwali Pahat in the city, said signboards are an effective way to reach voters, besides offering prayers to cows.

"Vasubaras is an event to offer prayers to cows. Politicians have sponsored such prayers. As cows are hard to find in the cities, they have found it a very good opportunity to reach out to voters by arranging for the cows," he said.

Mahajan said Deepotsav, the lighting up panatis, is also seen as an effective way to reach people. "Deepotsav is held at almost every chowk. Citizens turn up in large numbers. This helps politicians reach out to them at one place," he said.

Former Congress corporator Satish Desai, considered a pioneer of 'Diwali Pahat', admitted that to some extent the event is used for image building by politicians.

"But the basic idea should be to bring citizens together," he said.

"We started 'Diwali Pahat' with the same idea 17 years back. We felicitate businessmen who contributed to the city's development. And now the concept is going abroad. Marathi people in London, Muscat and Dubai are arranging 'Diwali Pahat' this year," he said.

Gala time for artistes too

The cultural programmes being held for five days will cost over Rs 3 crore. Performers like Shankar Mahadevan and Asha Bhosale will be in the city. Artistes have a huge demand next week. The budgets range from Rs 25,000 to Rs 1 lakh. "I was booked one-and-a-half-month in advance for three Diwali programmes next week. The demand is huge," said singer Chandrashekhar Mahamuni of Nishad, a musical group.

Heading: Hospitals on standby mode - Indian Express
Content:
HIV-positive patients under treatment who are showing signs of stability, can cut their mandatory travels to Pune from far flung places, with five new link antiretroviral treatment (ART) centres set to come up at Baramati, Manchar, Wadgao Maval, Indapur and Bhor.

Patients responding well to treatment can avail themselves of drugs from the link ART centres to be set up soon.

"We are already shifting drugs to these centres and have trained counsellors and medical officers," officials at the ART centre of Sassoon General Hospital said. This is part of the plan to have 36 link ART centres across the state, said Dr Rekha Jain, National AIDS Control Organisation's Western region coordinator.

Pune's first ART centre was set up at Sassoon General Hospital four years back and while 16,000 patients enrolled for medication, 6,000 were eligible for drugs. Later, as other ART centres were set up at Ahmednagar, Satara and other places, the load on Sassoon was reduced. At present, only 4,100 patients are on antiretroviral treatment here.

Now, a patient from Baramati will no longer need to visit Sassoon every month for the drugs as the link centre at the tehsil will ensure the supply. This facility will be useful for patients who have responded well to months of treatment and need not visit Sassoon for a check up. Similar link centres are being set up around Sangli, Mumbai and other places where the ART centres were initially set up, Jain said.

The initiative will go beyond the link ART centres as plans are on to set up centres in each district.

In Maharashtra, 1.2 lakh people are on antiretroviral treatment and 43,000 get the drugs. The government has a budget of Rs 40-50 crore for setting up these centres, complete with drugs and trained manpower. A camp will be held on November 6-7 in Mumbai to train medical officers before rolling out the plan.

Heading: HUDA’s land plan eats into DLF Garden City project pie - Indian Express
Content:
High alert: Deploy additional staff to deal with emergency cases

Diwali 2007: Nearly 150 people landed in the three major hospitals of the city — PGI, GMSH-16 and GMCH-32 — with burns and eye injuries sustained during the celebrations. Four of them completely lost vision in one eye. Most of those admitted were either children playing with crackers without the guidance of their elders or people hit by flying rockets while walking on roads.

Diwali 2006: As many as 107 patients in and around Chandigarh had to be taken to hospitals after receiving burns and other injuries while bursting crackers. Most of them were children.

Despite awareness drives, educational programmes and a growing concern over the high levels of pollution emitted from crackers, there has been no decline in the number of Diwali casualties. With two days to go before the Festival of Lights, city hospitals have started deploying additional staff, changing the rosters of doctors and announcing helplines to take care of the patient load.

"We have been receiving 18 to 20 cases of eye injuries every year, of which four are generally of serious nature causing long-term damage. This time, we have engaged one of our doctors in the advocacy programmes in schools to tell children how to celebrate a safe Diwali. But despite all these awareness programmes organised before the festival, if parents or other elders are not by the children's side as they burst crackers, the latter remain at risk," says Dr Sunandan Sood, head of the Department of Opthalomogy, GMCH-32.

The hospitals have already started receiving cases of cracker and bow-and-arrow injuries. "We had two such cases during Dusshera and it's just a matter of another day when more such cases will start pouring in," added Dr Sood.

Like the PGI's Advanced Eye Centre, which has prepared a special duty roster and circulated its emergency helpline numbers to address the Diwali patients, GMCH, too, will have doctors manning the emergency ward round the clock to take care of the patient load on Diwali.

At GMSH-16, which received nearly 100 cases of injuries last year, the medical staff will be reshuffled to spruce up the emergency services related to burns and face injuries. "Sufficient beds are already in place to deal with any rush of patients," said Dr S K Bhandari, the joint medical superintendent.

The Advanced Eye Centre at PGI will deploy additional staff to deal with the cases. "We have made elaborate arrangements to meet emergencies and provide immediate treatment to the patients. The department has put doctors on special emergency duty round the clock at the Advanced Eye Centre from October 27, 2008, till the morning of October 29, 2008," said a PGI official.

OPDs closed on Tuesday
OPDs at PGI, GMCH-32 and GMSH-16 will be closed on Tuesday, October 28, on account of Diwali. Emergency services in the three hospitals will, however, remain open with special staff on duty to deal with burns and eye injury cases.

Emergency Mobile No.: 9814014464

* At GMCH-32, the hotline number for eye injury cases is 98148-21212

* GMSH-16: Emergency can be reached at 102 (landline) and 0172-2768201, 202. For enquiries dial 0172-2782457

Precautions in case of emergency

* Light crackers with a candle, from a safe distance of 2-3 feet. Parents must accompany the children while bursting crackers

* Wear protective glasses so that particles from the crackers do not damage eyes. Do not rub eyes in case a foreign particle enters them

* In case of an eye injury, do not eat or drink anything before going to the doctor. The patient may need to have an empty stomach in case he or she has to undergo a minor operation

Heading: Stay on installation of mobile towers in residential areas scrapped - Indian Express
Content:
With the Haryana Urban Development Authority (HUDA) issuing a notification to acquire a big patch of land adjoining Amravati Enclave on the Pinjore-Kalka Road, the upcoming residential township project of the DLF may run into troubled waters. The DLF had earlier proposed to come up with Garden City, spread over 200 acres in the same area, the licence application for which has been pending with the Haryana Town and Country Planning Department for a long time now.

HUDA issued the notification recently to acquire the entire land from Amravati Enclave to Pinjore for the proposed Pinjore-Kalka urban complex.

On the other hand, the DLF claims to have already acquired more than 150 acres out of the required 200 acres for the project at a cost of around Rs 1 crore per acre, while the government rates are only around Rs 25 lakh for acre.

"As HUDA is to come up with an urban complex, a notification has been issued for acquiring land on which around 31 new sectors will be developed. The moment we receive the go-ahead, the process of acquisition will start. Though the DLF had plans to come up with a residential township on this land, they have not received the licence for it yet," said a senior HUDA official on the condition of anonymity.

DLF officials, however, said that though HUDA has issued the notification under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act, they are hopeful of getting its licence approved as they had applied for it much earlier. "We have acquired the land in that area and applied for the licence long ago. We hope there won't be any problem," said a DLF official who did not want to be named.

He added that an objection under Section 5A of the Land Acquisition Act had been filed by the DLF. "Once a land is notified under Section 4 of the relevant Act, the owners of the land in question and other people whose land is acquired can file their objections under Section 5A," said the official.

WHAT THEY SAY
"We now want to go ahead with the acquisition of land for the Pinjore-Kalka urban complex for which a notification under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act has been issued.

— A senior official of HUDA

"The government always reserves the right to acquire land. While HUDA has issued a notification, the DLF has also applied for a licence. It will now be the government which will decide as to whether the licence will be granted to the DLF or the HUDA will be given the go ahead to acquire land."
— S S Dhillon, Director, Town and Country Planning Department

"Though it has been more than one and a half year now since we applied for the licence, we will get the go-ahead soon. Also, we have filed objections under Section 5A against the HUDA notification to acquire land in that area."
— A DLF official

Heading: 3 dead, 1 injured in four mishaps in Mohali - Indian Express
Content:
Holding that there is no material on record to prove that the installation of mobile towers in residential areas is hazardous to the health, the Punjab and Haryana High Court has dismissed a bunch of petitions seeking stay on the setting up of mobile towers in inhabited areas.

A number of petitions, including a public interest litigation (PIL), was dismissed after the petitioners failed to produce any material on record which could prove that installation of mobile towers in residential areas is perilous to health. Though the counsel for the petitioners produced a couple of scientific studies and surveys, the said studies did not substantiate the claims of petitioners.

The counsel for mobile tower companies initially demanded the adjournment of case sine die, but when the court raised the question that if there was any material available to prove the apprehension correct, the counsels countered the claim mentioning a WHO report which claims that putting up a tower is not harmful to anyone's wellbeing.

"What material is available on record to prove this apprehension? Mobile towers only emit waves. When we are talking to you, it's the waves which are reaching to you, are they harmful to you?" questioned Chief Justice Tirath Singh Thakur.

Raising another point the petitioners submitted that the mobile tower companies have not sought No-objection Certificate (NOC) from the concerned municipal corporations. Showing no conviction in the averment, the Chief Justice held that as far as NOCs are concerned with regard to noise and other pollution, the same can be checked by the concerned municipal corporations. "There is no need to grant stay on the installation of mobile towers," he said.

With dozens of petitions pending in the Supreme Court, a PIL was filed in the Punjab and Haryana High Court in 2004, which stayed the installation of mobile towers in the residential areas.

Aggrieved, Cellular Operator Association of India had moved the Supreme Court, which stayed the order of the High Court.

The bunch of petitions had again come up for resumed hearing before the High court last week. Refusing to adjourn the petitions solely on the ground that similar petitions were pending in the Supreme Court, the High Court dismissed the petitions. However, the High Court has given the liberty to the petitioners to approach the court whenever any material proving and substantiating the allegations of damage being caused by the installation of mobile towers in residential areas is available.

Heading: Sector 18 plagued by encroachment and inadequate parking space - Indian Express
Content:
Two men and a woman lost their lives, while another woman sustained injuries, in separate road accidents in Kharar and Lalru areas of Mohali in the last 24 hours, police said on Saturday.

Kamla Devi, 65, and a resident of Raipur Kalan village near Mohali, was run over by a "recklessly driven" truck on the Kharar-Banur Road near Khalsa School in Kharar on Saturday.

Kamla was crossing the road when the truck, which was coming towards Banur from Kharar, hit her, the police said, adding that the woman died on the spot while the driver managed to flee. The accident occurred around 1 pm.

In another accident, Makhan Singh of Brahman Wala village near Kharar died when a bus from the Indo-Global College in Abhipur village near Kharar hit a motorcycle that Singh was riding. The accident took place on Saturday morning on the Chandigarh-Mullanpur Road near Hoshiarpur village. The speeding bus collided head-on with the bike, said the police, adding that Singh was rushed to PGIMER, where he succumbed to his injuries.

In Lalru, Baljinder Singh died when a recklessly driven tractor hit his motorcycle near Satarpur village. Police said it was a head-on collision. Singh was taken to GMCH-32, where he died.

In the fourth accident of the day, Darshan Kaur of Kharar sustained serious injuries when a truck trailer hit the Honda Activa scooter she was riding pillion from behind. It was around 7.45 pm and Kaur was returning home with her husband Avtar Singh from Daon village.

The police have registered separate cases of causing death and injuries due to negligence against the drivers of the offending vehicles.

Heading: Two die in separate road mishaps - Indian Express
Content:
The residents of Sector 18 are faced with the problems of poor roads and inadequate parking space.

"Some measures need to be implemented to prevent chaos due to the haphazardly parked vehicles. The problem persists both in the markets as well as residential areas. There are rows of cars parked on the roads. It makes it difficult for vehicles to pass," says a resident.

Another resident rues that construction waste is dumped at various places, including parks. "The parks are not well-maintained. Heaps of construction waste can be found at various places. Though there is a fine imposed on those who dump debris, it does not seem to be a deterrent."

The conditions of back lanes also leave a lot to be desired in terms of cleanliness. With garbage dumped almost everywhere and overgrown weeds creeping all around, these back lanes wear a dismal look.

The condition of the markets, particularly the booth markets, needs to be improved. The flooring of the market has to be revamped. With broken tiles, waterlogging is a common phenomenon making life difficult for pedestrians.

Encroachment is another problem area. Though a number of encroachment drives have been held time and again, they have invariably ended in tussles between the enforcement staff and shopowners.

Councillorspeak
Area councillor Anju Beniwala says there are a number of projects going on in the sector. "The parks are being developed. The roads were recarpetted recently. Paver blocks are also being laid in the booth markets. The facilities in the sector will be upgraded," added Beniwala.

Heading: Police-drug mafia nexus: S-I quizzed for 11 hours - Indian Express
Content:
Two persons died in separate road mishaps in the Zirakpur area on Saturday morning. In the first incident, a resident of Penta Homes, Zirakpur, died after a truck crushed the rickshaw in which he was travelling with his brother near Baltana T-point on the Zirakpur-Kalka highway around 11 am today. While Jeevraj Guatam (28) died on the spot, his brother escaped unhurt.

The traffic police officials nabbed the driver against whom a case was later registered by the Zirakpur police. In the other incident, an unidentified 60-year-old man was crushed to death by an unknown vehicle near Richmond Garden on the Ambala-Chandigarh highway around 7 am. The body has been sent for postmortem and the police have started investigations.

Man dies under mysterious circumstances
A thirty-four-year-old man, employed as a truck driver with the Empire Packages factory, died under mysterious circumstances on Saturday. Sukhwinder Singh, a resident of Rampur Chhat had left for Baddi on Thursday for the supply of factory goods. He was found unconscious in the cabin of the truck, parked along the highway near the Old Ghaggar Bridge, on Saturday morning. Sukhwinder was rushed to the Dera Bassi civil hospital from where he was shifted to the GMCH, Chandigarh, where he breathed his last. The body was sent for postmortem and the police have registered a case under Section 174 of the CrPC.

Youth dies after being hit by speeding car
CHANDIGARH: One youth died and three others sustained injuries after a driver, under the influence of liquor, hit their two-wheelers with his car at the dividing road of Sector 17 and 18 on Friday night. The deceased identified as Harpreet Singh (24) was a resident of Sector 61. Another youth Amit (25) fractured his hand. The other two — Lakhbir and Sunny — sustained minor injuries. Harpreet was working with a private firm for the past two years. He is survived by his mother and younger sister.
Police said Harpreet and Lakhbir were returning home on a Pulsar motorcycle. There were two more youths — Amit and Sunny — riding their Honda Activa scooter racing with Harpreet. Suddenly, a speeding Fiat Palio car (DL-2CQ-0324) hit both the two-wheelers from behind. All four fell on the road and sustained injuries.
Harpreet sustained head injuries and started bleeding profusely. A passerby informed the police. The victims were immediately rushed to hospital where Harpreet Singh breathed his last. The police arrested the driver, Gaurav Kaushik, a resident of Sector 22, on charges of rash driving and causing death due to negligence. He was later bailed out.
Police said eyewitnesses told them that Gaurav was driving recklessly and was at high speed. He did not apply the brakes when he noticed the two-wheelers in front of his car and hit them. The driver was tested and found to be driving under the influence of liquor. The body of the deceased was handed over to the family after conducting the postmortem.

Heading: Using ‘plea bargain’, Lok Adalat releases 45 undertrials - Indian Express
Content:
The officials with the Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB) interrogated Sub-Inspector Harinder Singh Sekhon for over 11 hours on Friday night in the alleged police-drug peddler nexus.

The sub-inspector was quizzed on his assets and that of his seniors and also their involvement in the alleged nexus.

"We are more concerned about the involvement of senior police officers.

We have asked whether the senior officers he had served with, were aware of his nexus with the drug peddlers. We are investigating the entire network and it appears difficult for a Sub-Inspector in the Chandigarh Police to carry out such activities without the involvement of senior officers," said an NCB officer.

The interrogation at the Zonal Headquarters, Sector 2, went on till 2 am as the NCB recorded all the proceedings of the investigations on the camera.

Zonal Director of the NCB Saji Mohan said they were examining the statements of Sekhon but refused to comment further. "Disclosing anything about the case would hamper investigations," said Mohan.

Drug peddler Raju, who was arrested nearly two months ago by the NCB, had alleged that S-I Sekhon helped him in his narcotics business in exchange of heavy purse. Also, the peddler apparently used the high profile network of the officer to sell drugs.

Heading: Phari Market traders unhappy with MC’s no-Diwali-stall decision - Indian Express
Content:
Forty-five undertrials, serving jail terms for various petty crimes, were released on Saturday after their cases were disposed off in the Mega Lok Adalat held under the concept of "Plea Bargain". The concept was introduced by making an amendment in the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) and brought into force on July 5, 2006. The Mega Lok Adalat also resolved 210 criminal cases using the concept of "Plea Bargain".

Those released had been booked for petty crimes under Sections 279 and 411 of the IPC, Excise Act and Gambling Act.

As per Section 265 (A to L) of the CrPC, "A person accused of an offence may file an application for plea bargaining in the court."

According to the CrPC provisions, "the magistrate shall take cognisance of an offence on complaint, other than an offence for which a term of death, life imprisonment or imprisonment more than seven years has been provided under the law. After receiving the application under sub-section (1), the court shall issue notices to the public prosecutor or complainant.

The orders would be pronounced as per Section 265-E of CrPC. No appeal can be filed except a Special Leave Petition in any court against such judgment."

Those released, meanwhile, expressed their happiness after their cases were disposed off.

"If not for this, we could have been visiting the courts, year after year, for the petty crimes we had committed," said one of the undertrials.

Heading: Non-veg food stalls in Sector 18-C pose serious problems for residents - Indian Express
Content:
The members of the Sector 17 Phari Market Union lamented that the Municipal Corporation (MC) didn't allow them to set up stalls in Sector 17. The union had demanded permission for Display Space Area for three days for Diwali only.

The issue came up for discussion during the Finance and Contract Committee meeting of the MC held this month and was then referred to the House. The union then filed a case in the court.

Harish Bansal, the general secretary of the union, said: "The next date of hearing has been fixed for October 29. It means that we will not be able to set up stalls before Diwali. While the MC has allowed stalls to be set up in every sector, we are being discriminated against."

Subhash Kataria, president of the Sector 17 Traders' Association, said that the issue has been politicised. "When the agenda was taken to the House by the Mayor, the councillors gave their approval. However, due to the intervention of the officials, the permission was not granted.

The traders in the sector had no objection towards the Phari Union setting up stalls," he says.

Heading: DAV College professors allege manhandling at principal’s behest - Indian Express
Content:
The Social Welfare Society, in Sector 18-C, has expressed concern over the presence of a rehri market in the area earmarked for a green belt. The members claim the stalls have become a nuisance for the residents. While the market has been there for some time, booths have been constructed in order to accommodate these shops. However, some shopkeepers have still not shifted to their assigned booths.

Coordinator Rakesh Arora says: "Some shopowners are declining that the Administration has allotted shops to them. These shops sell non-vegetarian food items till late in the night. The customers who generally come here indulge in drinking and smoking."

The members rued that due to the presence of these shops, stray dogs and scavengers frequently throng the area.

The shops also allegedly draw power from the electricity poles through unauthorised connections.

Parking is another major problem due to these stalls as vehicles parked outside them block the roads.

Area councillor Anju Beniwala said that the Administration should take steps to remove the stalls as it comes under their purview.

Heading: Promoting Sanskrit: Scholarship scheme draws mild response from students - Indian Express
Content:
A group of outsiders, allegedly acting on behest of Principal B C Josan of DAV College, manhandled the leadership of the DAV College Employees' Union on Friday evening.

The union members had boycotted a Diwali function called by the principal. Those manhandled include: President of the DAV College Teachers' Union Professor A K Taneja, Secretary of the DAV College Teachers' Union Professor Anil Sarwal, President of the Union and Staff Secretary Professor Avanindra Chopra and President Non-Teaching Employees' Union Som Nath.

In separate complaints filed with the President of the DAV College management, the vice-chancellor of Panjab University and the Director Higher Education, UT Administration, the union members have urged them to intervene in the matter and take immediate steps to check such acts of "intimidation" by the principal.

President of the DAV College Teachers' Union Professor A K Taneja said, "The representatives of the union along with the staff secretary had been meeting the Principal to chalk out the modalities for arranging a farewell function for nearly fifteen employees, awaiting a farewell since April 2007."

Taneja further added, "Yesterday, the principal went ahead and unilaterally announced a Diwali dinner on the same evening without any farewell function. The leadership had hoped that the Diwali dinner would also see a proper farewell for their colleagues but because this did not happen, the Union Executive decided to boycott the function."

Secretary of the DAV College Teachers' Union, Professor Anil Sarwal further said, "When Professor Taneja, Professor Avanindra Chopra and Som Nath were in the official union room in the evening, Principal Josan accompanied by nearly seven outsiders barged into the room and threatened them with dire consequences. He even pushed and shoved Professor Chopra who attempted to pacify the very aggressive intruders."

"As if this was not enough, when I arrived, I was heckled in the college parking lot by a group of outsiders acting on the behest of the principal. A couple of them advanced towards me using the filthiest and most abusive language and tried to physically

assault me. All this time, Josan continued to threaten us with dire consequences," alleged Sarwal.

Expressing his disappointment on the incident, Professor Chopra, said, "This is our Black Diwali. Such violent behaviour from the college principal has stunned us. Perhaps this is an aftermath of our successful struggle for CPF and leave encashment."

Chopra added, "We have also been trying to bring to the notice of the college authorities the gross irregularities in the college admissions and some other instances of mismanagement in the college. All this has enraged the principal who has acted in the most unbecoming manner."

While speaking to Newsline, Director Higher Education (DHE) Raji P Shrivastava, however, maintained that she has not received any complaint in the matter from any member of the DAV College Teachers' Union.

Heading: One-child norm generating ‘avoidance behaviour’ in children, say psychiatrists - Indian Express
Content:
The scholarship scheme introduced by the Ministry of Human Resources Development, Department of Higher Education, Government of India, to promote Sanskrit has received a lukewarm response from schools in the city.

School authorities, however, hold the Education department responsible for not creating enough awareness about the plan.

According to the scheme, students of Class IX and X, who scored 60 per cent and above in Sanskrit in Class VIII, receive a stipend of Rs 250 per month. For students of Class XI and XII, the amount is Rs 300 per month under the same scheme.

The Education department had sent directions to all the schools last year to shortlist meritorious students for the scholarship. "Last year we had nearly 40 students from our school receiving the scholarship. All the other schools had almost the same number of students who were eligible for the scheme," says Dr Vinod Sharma of Government Model Senior Secondary School, Sector 18.

This year, however, the department has not received any entries for the scholarship. The school

authorities blame it on the Department for not sending any intimation this year.

"Since the department had given information to all the schools last year, the scheme was a success. We are yet to receive any information from the department this year," says the principal of a government school.

Teachers believe the department should emphasise on creating awareness about the scholarship.

"It is a good step by the government to preserve the ancient language of Sanskrit. Schemes like these will help generate interest in the students about the subject, apart from benefiting them monetarily", said Dr Sharma.

Director Public Instructions (Schools) Samwartak Singh said the department is aware of the plan and is putting efforts to implement them in city schools. "We have sent out directions to schools to shortlist the deserving candidates and have asked them to give us the details immediately," said Singh.

Heading: A brush with art - Indian Express
Content:
A student of Class VI refused to attend school after being slapped by his teacher. A psychiatrist was needed after the child went into depression. In another incident, a student stopped going to school after being punished for not completing his homework. He joined school only after being counselled by a clinical psychologist. These are not isolated incidents.

According to Dr B S Chavan, Head of the department, Psychiatry, GMCH-32, children these days have become increasingly sensitive to criticism, which explains why they are unable to accept even mild reactions from teachers.

"In the current academic session only, I have counselled as many as five children indulging in avoidance behaviour after being reprimanded by their teachers. In all the cases, children consciously avoided going to school as they felt insulted and took everything to heart," says Dr Chavan.

Talking to Newsline, the mother of a child being counselled by Dr Chavan says, "After slapping my son in the class, the teacher turned him out of the classroom which was too much for him to bear. While the incident took place in April, I came to know about it only in June, when he declined to attend school after summer vacations."

She adds, "He used to have disturbed sleep and his behaviour had also changed. If one moment he cried without any provocation, the very next second he was seen laughing. It was then that we decided to seek professional help."

According to Dr Chavan, the one-child norm and nuclear families are largely responsible for producing a breed of extra-emotional children.

"Earlier when there were joint families, some uncle or aunt used to scold children, which in a way prepared them for harsh treatment. Now, with only one or two children, they are over-protected by parents, which makes them more vulnerable to be easily hurt," says the doctor.

Dr Chavan suggests that parents should acquaint their children with the harsh realities of life. "Children should be taught to face the grimmest of situations and not succumb to them. They need to be prepared for the journey called life at an appropriate time," concludes Dr Chavan.

Heading: 'Cause we care - Indian Express
Content:
City's canvas gets a masterstroke of class and taste at the newly-opened Gallery Art 17

Like the phoenix, this too has risen from the ashes, not once, but thrice. Three's a lucky charm and gallery Art 17's finally opened its artistic doors to Chandigarh folks. "I would define it as a natural progression to our profession...photography is a form of art," Tej Bans Singh Jauhar sits back and takes a long look at his gallery housed at Tejee Studios in Sector 17, a dream, which has realised after years.

A connoisseur, Tej Bans rewinds to the year 1964 when he, along with his elder brother, had started the 'first of its kind art gallery in the region.' "Adarsh Applied Arts and Advertising Agency," nostalgia sweeps his face. But due to lack of awareness, the gallery ran into rough weather and had to be shut down. "Guess it came much before its time." What are priceless brands today were nameless struggling artists of that era. "Nobody understood art, there was lack of exposure," recalls Tej Bans. But Chandigarh's come a long way since then. People have realised the importance of interiors and that there's art beyond crystal-ware. In the meantime, Jauhar could never put out the fire in his belly. The gallery was given a second shot with Shiv Singh's exhibition some seven-eight years back, but "suddenly, space became expensive in Sector 17, and the dream died again." Only to resurface, this time, for sure. And giving him a push is his son, Munish Jauhar, bringing the dream back to life. "We've christened it as Art 17," he smiles with pride, as Munish shows us around an impressive collection of art works from all over the country. "Shobha Broota, T Waikuntam, K Laxma Goud, Ramesh Gorjala, Shiv Singh..." Munish goes through the available works, an A-list promising to paint the pale palette of the city with a riot of colour that spells class and taste. "Our aim is to bring in emerging, up and coming Indian artists, and sensitise people about art," Munish's a votary for creating awareness on this invaluable asset. "Art is increasingly turning into quite an investment," he asserts, hinting at an exhibition before the year end. If you are looking for a collector's item, or a specific piece of work, Art 17 can arrange that too. "We can source it from personal collections, it all depends on how you traverse your network," Munish, Founder CEO of Gray Cell Technologies, is enjoying this fine marriage of the internet, software and art. "Another thing, we are not restricted to just paintings, there are photographs and sculptures too," he chips in. "The USP? Well, it's a small gallery with a big reputation," Tej Bans gives the masterstroke. For more, log on to www.art17.in.

Heading: Dim Diwali - Indian Express
Content:
West Bengal Pollution Control Board (WBPCB) has issued a six-month ultimatum to 31 industrial units in Durgapur, the industrial hub of the state, to reduce smoke emissions.

Under the banner of Operation Clear Sky-Durgapur, WBPCB scientists have compiled a research study highlighting the deteriorating quality of the air in Durgapur.

"In our survey, we found the environment of the Durgapur Municipal area has visible emissions from industries. With the health of more than 500,000 residents at stake, it is important that we take some action to reduce the level of emissions," said Dipak Chakraborty, chief scientist, WBPCB.

"If the industries fail to stick to the timeline, strict action will be taken against them," Chakraborty added.

According to the survey, industrial areas in and around the Durgapur Municipal area, especially on the southern side of NH-2 (G T Road), have been major contributors to the rising pollution level of the industrial town.

The study pegs the level of respirable particulate matter (RPM) in Durgapur to be constantly increasing and way above the national standard. The survey says the RPM level at Durgapur stood at 114 mg/m3 in 2007, almost double the normal level of 60 mg/m3.

"The nitrogen dioxide level is also increasing. As per our research, we have found the current level of nitrogen dioxide in Durgapur stands at 51.5 mg/m3," said a WBPCB official.

Some of the major polluting industries identified in the survey are Durgapur Steel Plant, Alloy Steel Plant, Durgapur Projects Ltd (DPL), Durgapur Thermal Power Station (DTPS) and NTPC-SAIL Power Supply Corporation Ltd (NSPCL).

According to the study, sponge iron units like Shyam Steel Industries Ltd, Haldia Steel Ltd, CP Sponge Ltd, Ritesh Tradefin Ltd and SPS Steel & Power Ltd are some of the other units harming the environment of Durgapur.

The survey also lists Sova Ispat Ltd, Srinivasa Ferro Alloy Ltd, Haldia Steel Ltd, Durgapur Chemicals Ltd, Philips Carbon Black Ltd and Graphite India Ltd among others whose emissions are detrimental to the air quality of the industrial town.

According to experts, cement industries, mini blast furnaces, fuel coke manufacturers, coal tar distillation units, mining activities, mine pit fire in neighbouring mine areas are other sources identified as air pollutants.

The WBPCB has already conducted a meet with the leading industrial units of Durgapur.

The second round of the meeting to review the progress made by industries in controlling smoke emissions is scheduled in November.

Heading: Car enters IGI airside without permit - Indian Express
Content:
With slowdown, retrenchment, and general cost-cutting in the industry and tightening budget driving the home front, Sandeep Bansal, whose company specialises in customised gifts, was sort of expecting a slump. But a 50-per

cent drop in Diwali gift orders this year caught him unawares.

Usually, he says, the orders peaked at Rs 1 crore for corporate gift items over the past three or four years. It has barely touched Rs 40 lakh this year, Bansal says.

"This is unprecedented," he says, "we have no one to blame, though."

At least 30 companies that placed orders with Chemzone India, which customises gift items from local manufacturers scattered in Faridabad and Ghaziabad, did not come shopping this year, Bansal says. About 20 clients cancelled part of their orders, and those who did place orders for corporate gifts opted for cheaper options such as leather wallets, mobile accessories and key chains that cost up to Rs 200, he says.

Brass products were also in demand as these came for less than Rs 800, another gift manufacturer says. There was also a huge demand for steel gift items and home utilities as these were innovative and a relatively newer concept, the manufacturer says.

For local manufactures, this Diwali season has been a nightmare. While retailers have been cautious and only bought what has been ordered in advance, for manufacturers who have stocked their inventory in anticipation, the losses are substantial.

Subhash Sabharwal of Creative Candles, a company that makes candles and chocolate gift hampers, says business this season is down 25 per cent compared to last year. The shelf life of candles isn't long and they won't last till the next year, he says.

"Diwali is not the same this year," Sabharwal said. "This is the biggest slump I have seen in eight years. Hamara toh lakhon ka nuksaan hai."

Cutting losses not easy
Many importers, too, are stuck with gift items from China that are not selling. There is just no demand, says Sabharwal. While 'gift gurus' say a cheap gift on the occasion must be avoided as employees look forward to these, for companies struggling with the slowdown, cost-cutting is one way to stay afloat. Mukul Anand (name changed on request), who works for a reputed communications firm, says he was expecting designer diyas instead of the box of sweet that he got from his office as Diwali gift. "The ladoos are bad," he says.
But business isn't that bad for some manufacturers. Naveen Patel, whose company manufactures and supplies silver coins and such gift items, is not complaining. Since silver prices took a beating — current prices are about Rs 16,500 per kg — there is a surge in demand for 10-gram silver coins that cost Rs 200 each. The last word? "It's actually better than last year."

Heading: Man held for killing realtor opposed to his affair - Indian Express
Content:
In a major security breach at the IGI Airport, a Toyota Qaulis drove past the cargo gate of the domestic terminal without requisite licence or pass on Friday night.

The incident reportedly occurred at 1.25 am Saturday, with CISF officers guarding the cargo gate not questioning the two occupants of the MUV.

An airport official, who did not want to be identified, said the employees of private firm Sahara Press drove up in a white Qualis (DL5EA3783) around 1 am. First-timers at the airport, they assumed it is normal practice to drive in since there was no one to question them at the cargo gate, the official said.

The duo — R S Yadav, supervisor, and Sishupal, a housekeeping staff — has told officials that they were at the airport to pick up a consignment from Kingfisher cargo. According to officials, no case has been registered. The duo was let off after questioning; they were not arrested.

Each vehicle entering the airport needs a vehicle permit issued by DIAL and only a specified number of permits are issued to check traffic on the airside. Each occupant of the vehicle also needs an airport entry permit, issued by the Bureau of Civil Aviation Security. This could be temporary as well as permanent.

It is also mandatory for a driver to possess an airport driving permit. Issued by GMR, it is given only after proper training in which the driver is told about driving inside the premises, speed limits, and the need to stick to designated routes among others.

An Indian Airline official reportedly spotted Yadav and Sishupal at hangar number 2, where Indian Airlines aircraft are parked for maintenance. The Indian Airlines official informed the CISF control room, and the two were picked up for questioning by Delhi Police.

The CISF spokesperson could not be contacted despite repeated attempts.

"Two aircraft were parked at the hangar at the time and at least another six were parked close by," an airport official said.

What you need
* Vehicle permit issued by GMR for entry
* Airport entry permit for each occupant of the vehicle
* Airport driving permit issued by GMR for driver

Heading: Vodafone asked to pay up for disconnection - Indian Express
Content:
The Crime Branch on Friday arrested a 30-year-old history-sheeter from Haryana for killing an acquaintance of his girlfriend's mother.

Wanted in six cases across Haryana and Delhi, Robin Singh had pumped two bullets into Munna Singh, a property dealer, on September 12 outside the girl's house in Rohini Sector-17, the police said.

According to police, Robin told them during interrogation that he killed Munna because the latter was harassing Bhawna — a 25-year-old call centre employee he had fallen in love with. A murder case was registered against Robin after Bhawna's brother, 12, said he had seen him roaming the area on his motorcycle that morning.

Robin has told the police that Munna Singh knew Bhawna's mother, Renu Saini, for the past two years. They both were apparently opposed to his affair with Bhawna. "Munna allegedly threatened him (Robin) with dire consequences if he did not stop seeing her," DCP (Crime) Neeraj Thakur said. "The girl also told the accused that Munna had made advances towards her and was harassing her.

"This infuriated the accused and he decided to murder Munna."

According to police, Bhawna and Robin had eloped three times before and Munna had warned them about the consequences if they repeated the act one more time.

Haryana Police had earlier declared Robin a notorious criminal and declared a reward of Rs 5,000 for information leading to his arrest.

Heading: Ponting goes Meerut to shave bat - Indian Express
Content:
At a time when cellular network connectivity is just about average at the best of times comes an order from the consumer forum, asking a service provider to pay damages for playing erratic with a consumer's connection.

In a recent order, the Delhi Consumer Commission has directed mobile service provider Vodafone Essar Ltd to pay Rs 30,000 as compensation to a Rohini resident whose telephone connection was disconnected "without any reason".

"Legal remedies are becoming costlier by the day and going beyond the reach of the middle class, what to talk of a common man?" Commission president Justice J D Kapoor observed. "This fact should always be kept in mind by traders and services providers, who are rich and have sources to engage senior advocates only to avoid payment of a few thousands."

The observations came on an appeal filed by Vodafone against a district forum order asking the company to pay Rs 30,000 as damages. The cellular company had disconnected the services of Rohini resident Ajay Jain on three occasions in 2004 without, the complainant says, giving a notice or furnishing any reason.

Vodafone argued that the compensation amount was steep and that it had restored Jain's connection on all three occasions the same day it was disconnected. The Commission, however, dismissed the argument and directed the service provider to pay the damages for the "mental agony and harassment" suffered by Jain. The consumer panel has directed Vodafone to pay the compensation within a month.

Heading: Where the lights are still on - Indian Express
Content:
As the city gears up for Diwali, and then the all-important Test match at Feroze Shah Kotla, Australia skipper Ricky Ponting is busy getting a regional touch to regain his touch with the willow after the setback at Mohali.

Accompanied by wicketkeeper Brad Haddin, the 33-year-old from Tasmania made a whirlwind tour to Meerut on Thursday to shave the balance on his bat. The two spent some three hours at the SG bat factory in the city renowned for manufacturing sports goods on Thursday and ordered bats for themselves and teammates.

According to sources, they weighed features of each bat and suggested some modifications. Ponting reportedly ordered three bats for himself while Haddin chose two. They also ordered two bats each for teammates Shane Watson and left-handed bat Michael Hussey.

The cricketers and officials from the sports goods manufacturer did not speak with the media.

Incidentally, Ponting has had a wrist surgery due to which he missed the last home series against Bangladesh. He is on his first tour since the surgery and realised after the Chennai and, more specifically, Mohali Test matches that he needs to use his wrists a lot more on Indian wickets. According to information, he shaved the balance of the bat slightly to have less strain on his wrists.

Haddin came to inspect new wicketkeeping gloves.

Ponting, Haddin, Watson and Hussey — the last two did not come to Meerut — play with Kookaburra bats. SG manufactures the willows for Kookaburra and delivers them to Australia.

Heading: Skilled force - Indian Express
Content:
The festive buzz may be missing from malls and markets but in Old Delhi, the sparkle is still there

This festive season the buzz may be missing from malls and markets in the city but in old Delhi, the sparkle is still there. A bit dim perhaps, but not lost either. Its lanes are all lit and its halwais are busy making the sweets that have made Old Delhi a foodie's delight.

"You cannot bring in a festival without binging on some traditional sweets. It's part of our culture and people still prefer giving authentic Indian sweets rather than anything else," says one of the sellers at Chaina Ram. Judging by the number of customers his shop has, he's probably right.

At the famous jalebi shop in Dariba Kalan, samosas and piping hot jalebis fly off from the counter the moment they are put down. The shop's crowded as usual and owner Kailash Jain insists Diwali has not ushered in increased sales. Between taking orders and dishing out small change, he says, "There has been recession in the US, it is a difficult time for the country and business is low." The crowd of customers around his shop nod intelligently.

But Arvind Singh, who sits behind the hot iron-cast wok at the shop and serves jalebis and samosas every few minutes, is happy with the business. "I've been doing this for 24 years now. During the Diwali season, we begin the preparations at seven in the morning and usually finish by 11 or 12 at night," he says.

A few blocks inside Dariba Kalan, a jewellery shop has packed away its silverware. A makeshift platform has been put up. Ram Gopal and Sons have converted their shop into a kaleidoscope of colours with beautifully crafted idols from West Bengal on sale. Priced between Rs 20 and Rs 500, the idols of Ganesha and Lakshmi are decked in bright colours. "Every year on Diwali we sell these idols. It is not just about getting extra income, it also brings good luck," says Vinod Gupta.

Meghraj and Sons at Fatehpuri Road, who specialise in cashew pastries, have layered the corners of their shop with decorated gift boxes. "We usually get gift orders and store these packaging in advance," says one of the sellers. At Jain Sweets, kaju barfi is priced at Rs 220 a box and 700gms of Karanchi halwa at Rs 74.

At Khari Baoli, the famous dry fruit bazaar, the pavement is pockmarked with local fruit sellers who have taken to selling paper boxes and gold embellished fancy gift bags for the season. For anything between Rs 50 and Rs 1,000, you can get beautifully decorated boxes and pack them with dryfruits.

For Akram Qureshi, a fruit seller, Diwali is the best time of the year. His kiosk, a temporary structure made with cardboard boxes, is heaped with coconuts. "During the festival we sell just dry coconuts that we source from Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh. We sell about 2,000 of these," says Qureshi who has been putting up his coconut stall since 1972.

Heading: Photo shop - Indian Express
Content:
The Gunjan Foundation gives vocational training to girls from slums

Talking to the daughter of her sweeper three years ago, Sushma Singhvi saw just how keen she was to work and earn a living. Singhvi decided to teach her and girls like her pick some skills. She began teaching them how to make candles. Today, Singhvi heads Gunjan Foundation, an organisation that gives underprivileged women vocational training. "The foundation works towards empowering women. We provide them vocational training which polishes their craftsmanship," says Singhvi.

The foundation has its own vocational centre at Shahpur Jat, where the girls are trained for two to three months and learn to make a variety of products. "The merchandise that these girls learn to make include candles, bags, flowers and stuff toys among other things. The foundation then takes charge of marketing these goods," says Singhvi, who has buyers such as Rio Grande in Greater Kailash-1.

The foundation was started in 2003, but the first two years after its inception were dedicated to spreading awareness, through seminars such as 'Mind Pollution', which talked about restoring traditional and cultural elements in the process of becoming modern. A book on it will be released early next year.

But when it comes to spreading awareness among underprivileged women, it is the distribution of pamphlets in slums and word-of-mouth that works. "When one girl realises her dream and understands the importance of financial independence, the word automatically spreads and more people want to be a part of the programme," says Singhvi who started her career compering programmes like Patrika, Sahityaki and Bal Jagat on Doordarshan.

In the past three years, 40 women have enrolled under the programme and now earn up to Rs 400 a week. With Diwali just round the corner and with orders for candles hovering over 3,000, the girls have a lot to do. "The girls are paid for every item that they make and the amount then depends on the kind of hard work they are willing to do," says Singhvi.

But the real work begins even before the girls join work. The first big job is convincing their families. "Usually it's the brothers of these girls who are very traditional and don't them to go out of their homes. And the mothers of these girls worry that their daughters' marriage prospects will be hit if they work," says Singhvi.

But now that these girls are trained, they are putting their skills to good use, holding workshops in colleges, teaching interested students the craft that they have learnt.

Heading: The university line - Indian Express
Content:
A photo printing website does more than just print photos. It also customises merchandise

When Animesh Jain, 26, was working as a software engineer with an IT solutions company in Delhi and wanted to send photographs to his mother in Bangalore, he was in a fix. Getting the photographs printed in bulk would cost him a packet. He realised this must be a problem for many people. So, after a bit of brainstorming, this IIT Delhi graduate found a solution. He got a couple of his batchmates together and set up itasveer.com, a website where one can place orders for digital prints and get them delivered home. "I wanted to send hard copies of some photographs to my mother in Bangalore and the photo studios were charging exorbitantly. Add to it the additional cost of sending them by courier and I was already counting my change," says Jain, who quit his job a year ago to set up the website. A team of seven IIT Delhi graduates is involved in the process of constantly developing and improving the software on the website.

The website delivers digital quality photos anywhere in India in less than 24 hours with a follow-up system to ensure the photos reach the customer on time. All one needs to do is log on to the site and create an account, which ensures your privacy giving you a user name and password. One can then proceed to the "add photos" option that allows you to queue up the photos for printing. You can choose from the various sizes on offer and also customise the photograph by getting a picture caption printed on it. Their software, 'doodle pad', allows the user to take the photo and presentation format to make it as attractive as they want. For instance, one can customise a table calendar by placing the photo interestingly, changing the theme, using vibrant colours with different designs for each month of the year. Though this might come at an extra cost, Jain says it is worth it. "One would ordinarily buy a calendar for a couple of hundred rupees. But we give you the option of personalising your merchandise and making it much more special," he explains.

The charges for customisation fall between Rs 85 and Rs 1,000 and one can choose from mugs, calendars, cards, collages and mouse pads. The site plans to work on customised photo books next.

In the two years of its existence, the website has registered over 25,000 members. "We do not print the photographs at our office. We simply outsource them to a Mumbai photo studio that we have contracted for this purpose. Our servers instantly relay the customer's demand and within a short span of time, the snaps are dispatched to the desired address. We only follow up with the customer after a few days," says Ankit Khanna, co-founder of the site. The cost of printing a 4x6 photograph is Rs 2.90 with additional shipping charges. This site is useful for people with bulk orders since the packaging charges are in various slots with the minimum being Rs 50 for a set of 35 photographs of 4x6 size.

With other photo printing sites coming about, the techies are aware of the competition and are constantly upgrading their services. "We will soon start sending parcels abroad once we get the logistics sorted out," says Khanna.

Heading: CRPF constable, accomplice held for murder of 18-yr-old - Indian Express
Content:
Delhi University's Department of Geology has lent its expertise to the Delhi Metro

The metro line to Delhi University is not the campus's only link to the Delhi Metro. Since 2001, the university's Department of Geology has been giving invaluable backend expertise to the Delhi Metro Rail Corporation (DMRC), especially for the construction of underground lines.

"I feel proud to have contributed to the development of our city," says Dr Manoj Chowdhary, guest lecturer at the Geology Department. Before joining the department, Chowdhary was the chief geologist in Hindustan Zinc Ltd.

"Our association with the DMRC started well before Delhi even dreamt of having a metro," says Chowdhary who has recently completed a Ph.D in Earthquake Studies. "The Department of Science and Technology approached us to inspect the sub surface structure of the line between Viswavidyalaya and Central Secretariat, through drilled holes. We prepared a three-dimensional sub-surface structure so that they knew the hardness, grain size and texture of the soil well before the digging started.Instruments such as the GPR (Ground Penetration Radar) were used to scan the sub-surface till about 25 metres, says Prof C. S. Dubey of the Geological Department.

A geological fault was discovered in the Chawri Bazaar area and the DMRC was stuck at the same point for four months, remembers Chowdhary.

The Geology Department also prepared a sub-surface model for the whole city, which included geological and geotechnical modelling. Liquefaction hazard maps and seismic activity hazard maps too were prepared. The whole city was divided into four zones—from low/no risk to high-risk zones.

"This information was invaluable and essential for DMRC. The underground digging as well as the placement of the pillars was to be done keeping all this information in mind," adds Chowdhary. "During our research we found two faults running through Delhi which went unnoticed all this time. These two faults, one from Faridabad to Rohtak and the other from the Yamuna (near Red Fort) to Sonepat, put all the included area at a high risk to seismic activity.

Their work is not over yet. "At many places, construction of the metro is in its early stages and we will continue to work hand in hand with the DMRC," says Chowdhary. And what did he feel when he rode the metro? "Having been a part of this project is a matter of pride for me," says Chowdhary.

Apart from contributing to the building of the metro, the Geology Department has also provided geotechnical and geological analysis for all hydroelectric projects in India.

Heading: Festive rush fails to hot up in malls - Indian Express
Content:
A CRPF constable was arrested on Saturday from Southwest Delhi for the abduction and murder of an 18-year-old boy. Police officials said the victim, Sandeep Singh, had gone missing on October 1 while returning from his management institute in Janakpuri.

Police said the CRPF constable, identified as Sandeep and his friend Om Tyagi, belonged to Singh's village, Revla Khanpur. They knew his father, Dharambeer very well. Dharambeer had recently sold his plot for Rs 40 crore, which the constable and Tyagi were aware of.

Sources said after abducting the boy, they shot him the same day as the boy knew them. They abandoned his body near a well near the Jhatikhra police post under the newly-constructed Chawala police station.

Police said after the boy went missing, his family searched for him for days. When they got the first ransom call on October 10, they registered a police complaint.

"On October 11, they got a call from a PCO in Anand Vihar. On 13 October, the call was traced to Nandgram in Ghaziabad. Over the next three days, the calls were made from a PCO near Dabri police station. The kidnappers would repeatedly ask Dharambeer to come with Rs 40 lakh for the safe release of the boy. The calls were highly suspicious as they would not let Dharambeer talk to the abducted boy," a senior police officer said.

On Saturday, Dharambeer got another call from kidnappers, who asked him to arrive near Chawala with the ransom. A police team went with Dharambeer and arrested the two men. Constable Sandeep is with 88th Batallion, posted in Dwarka. A decomposed body of the boy also was recovered with their help.

Singh was pursuing his bachelors in Business Administration at a private institute in Janakpuri.

Heading: Teacher beats 13-year-old in govt school, fractures hand - Indian Express
Content:
With neon lights, brightly-lit shops, houses and offices, Gurgaon looks all ready to celebrate Diwali. Store owners at the malls however, say the rush is less compared to previous years.

"The malls in Gurgaon are usually choked this time of the year. Ours is crowded, but not as much as in previous years. We hope the rush will increase in the next two days. Security has been tightened but it is almost impossible to ensure the place will be 100 per cent secure," said Vijay Aima of Sahara Mall where Big Bazaar is a major crowd-puller.

"It is a mad rush in Big Bazaar. With so many discounts, people are just walking out with trolleys full of gifts.

"Big Bazaar has called in more staff from other centres to meet the growing rush here," added Aima.

When asked about the possible reason for the fall in sales this year, Brigadier Deepak Kapur, general manager, operations, Ambience Mall, said: "It is not so much the fear of terror attacks as the recent economic slowdown. People can not resist the temptation to shop and it is very likely that the rush will return in the coming days."

Visitors had their own explanations. Subham Chakroborty, an MNC executive said, "If a festival comes at the end of a month, we are almost out of funds. Companies are also on a cost-cutting drive and we have not got the expected bonus. This might be why most of my colleagues have tried to resist shopping this Diwali."

The police, on their part, have intensified security checks and are always on the alert in case of any emergency, said senior police officials.

Heading: Prices no damper, cracker sales sparkle - Indian Express
Content:
A 13-year-old boy was beaten by his Physical Education teacher in a government school in Mukherjee Nagar in Northwest Delhi on Friday afternoon, said the police. After medical reports showed he had fractured his hand, the police registered a criminal case against the teacher, who is on the run.

Police said the victim, Garvit, went home at 2.30 pm on Friday and fell unconscious. When he told his parents he was beaten by his teacher in school, they filed a complaint.

"The boy told us that some senior boys went to the spot and shouted obscenities at Ashok Chauhan, the teacher. When he turned around, the boys fled and Garvit was caught. Chauhan beat him with a stick. There were bruises on the boy's head too," a senior police officer said.

Garvit's mother took him to the principal and told her about the incident. Garvit again fell unconscious in the principal's room.

He was taken Bara Hindu Rao Hospital, where a medical examination showed he had fractured his hand.

By the time the principal summoned Chauhan, he had left.

A case was registered against Chauhan. Garvit lives with his parents in Dhaka Village in Mukherjee Nagar. He is a class VIII student of Rajkiya Senior Secondary School, officials added.

Heading: Happy with response, cops all out to woo ‘eyes and ears’ - Indian Express
Content:
While the prices of crackers have gone up due to increasing raw material costs and licensing issues, there has been no marked difference in sales at the large cracker shops.

At a licensed wholesale price shop near Filmistan hall, Karol Bagh, shoppers come from as far as Noida to purchase crackers.

Mantesh Nagar, an employee of the store, says the demand for crackers has not declined noticeably.

"Crackers will never go out of fashion," he says. "Children still buy a lot of phuljharis but the demand for rockets and crackers has gone up. Older people want the sparklers that shoot up in the sky and don't make much noise," says Nagar. "People want to buy new items. They keep asking us what is new in the market. Even if there are variations in colours or names, it sells," says Rajesh, who has stocked crackers at his shop in IP Extension, East Delhi for the week.

Most of the large wholesale shops remain closed through the year, and open only for the season after Dussehra. The government grants temporary licences to them for a fortnight or a month. The licensing procedure this year, however, has upset shop owners. S Kumar, who owns a large wholesale store in Karol Bagh, says the government delayed granting licences for crackers this year.

"Our sales pick up usually right after Dussehra. This time we could only open our shop a couple of days ago," he says, adding that the resulting last minute rush posed a safety hazard due to the crowd in the market.

The licence is issued through the area DCP but shop owners say that the beat police and fire department asked for large bribes to issue licences. "They said the government will not allow many shops this year, but they'll help us if we grease their palms," said a shop owner on condition of anonymity.

Heading: DIAL to open more food and beverage outlets at airport - Indian Express
Content:
In a plan to involve the public in curbing crime in the Capital before the Commonwealth Games, the focus is on the 'eyes and ears scheme' of the Delhi Police. As part of the scheme, lay people gather intelligence for the police.

In more than nine months now, after the scheme was launched by Commissioner Y S Dadwal in January, Delhi Police officials have held 41,037 meetings in all 11 districts with more than 75,000 people to encourage them to help the police and give information about criminals, criminal activities and to educate themselves about crime.

A toll-free helpline number, 1090, is working exclusively for the 'eyes and ears scheme'. People can report any information and their identities are kept confidential. Officers say as the scheme is a success, they want to increase its scale so that it becomes a landmark and a morale booster for police personnel, and a trendsetter for other police departments.

"This scheme is running on a big scale in all districts and we receive lot of information from people who are part of it. A hundred and twenty-nine cases have been solved with the help of the people till now and several criminals arrested," Rajan Bhagat, Delhi Police PRO, said. Officials said since senior officers and SHOs brief people about criminals, they are watchful and alert, and help the police.

The idea behind the scheme goes beyond collecting criminal intelligence. It is to increase public participation to prevent crime. Beat constables are playing a key role in this 'eyes and ears' scheme because they know their areas better. The briefing of such informers public is taken every week either by SHOs or ACPs. Even joint commissioners of police have participated in the briefings.

Police's partners
For information, the police looks to street vendors, rickshaw-pullers, chowkidars, RWAs, barbers, parking lot attendants, security guards of banks, private and government organisations, TSR/taxi drivers, bus drivers and conductors, cyber café owners, property agents, second-hand car dealers, guesthouse owners and porters at railway stations, ISBTs and airports. The scheme also includes Nagrik Suraksha Samitis, washerman, doctors in slums, barbers, plumbers, lock repairers, petrol pump workers, domestic help providers, mechanics, dairy booth operators, and dhabas.

Heading: Nepali national, 3 others held with fake currency - Indian Express
Content:
Recognising that their end consumer is not just passengers but also the people who come to drop and receive them, Delhi International Airport (P) Limited (DIAL) has now decided to develop more food and beverage outlets at the airport for all "palettes and wallets".
