DIAL is inviting Expressions of Interest (EoI) from interested parties for the setting up of operations, maintenance and management of such outlets at the under-construction new domestic departure terminal, Terminal 1-D, which will cater to full service airlines such as Jet Airways and low-cost carriers. The new terminal, expected to be ready by early next year, will take over from the existing departure terminal, Terminal 1-B.

"With the advent of low-cost carriers, which do not include meals in the ticket price, the number of passengers eating at airport outlets has gone up substantially. It is important that prices remain reasonable," Arun Arora, associate vice-president of corporate communications, DIAL, said.

"An important aspect of air travel in India is the many friends and relatives who come to pick or drop passengers at the airport. They are vital to the airport economy and it is important that proper facilities are provided for the visitors," an industry analyst said.

While IGI Airport already has more than 40 food and beverage outlets, DIAL is planning to open several new such outlets in near future. "These will be a mix of kiosks and take away, sit-down and fine dining restaurants, and will cater to all palettes and wallets," the official said.

"Reputed companies with extensive experience in running food and beverage outlets, especially in an airport environment, are expected to apply for this contract. The applicants must be reputed brand owners, brand franchisers or franchisees having multiple food and beverage concepts, with at least five years of continuous experience in setting up, operating and maintaining innovative outlets in India or abroad," a senior official said.

Major names like McDonalds, Subway, Nirulas, Yo China, Café Coffee Day and Costa Coffee, along with fine dining restaurants operated by India's leading hotel chains, the Welcome Group and Ashoka Hotels, are already present at the airport.

The new Terminal 1-D will have a capacity to handle on crore passengers per annum. The new building will be a two-level structure, where passengers will check-in at the upper level and proceed to the security hold area. The check-in process will be streamlined with the induction of an advanced in-line baggage handling system. This system will not only make check-in faster for passengers but make it more secure and efficient.

Heading: New traffic plan to rid Gurgaon of snarls - Indian Express
Content:
The West District police have arrested four persons, including a Nepali citizen, involved in a counterfeit currency racket in Delhi and Kolkata.

The accused have been identified as Mohammad Murtaza (29), Shoaib Ali (48), Dilawar Singh (47) and Mohammad Shamim (35). Shamim is a Nepali citizen and would procure the counterfeit notes from one Motilal, alias Malchu, in Nepal. The police are trying to trace all other people who are part of this racket.

The police said the counterfeit currency was procured by Shamim, who bought Rs one lakh in fake notes for Rs 50,000. One of the accused, Mohammad Murtaza, alias Samir, started smuggling fake notes some two years ago. The police have recovered Rs four lakh in counterfeit currency from their possession. The recovered notes are in the denomination of 500 and 1,000 rupee notes. "The counterfeited currency recovered is of high quality. No one can easily establish that it is fake," Sharad Aggarwal, DCP West District, said. The money was reportedly smuggled in from Bangladesh.

The accused were arrested from near Shivaji Palace in Rajouri Garden when they had gone there to deliver the counterfeit currency to somebody.

The main accused, Murtaza, earlier worked in a boutique in Rajouri Garden. "He came into contact with one Imtiaz in Kolkata and started the circulation of counterfeit currency. In January this year, he was arrested in Najafgarh and Rs 65,000 in counterfeit currency was recovered from him. Later, he came in contact with Shamim and also Dilawar, a moneylender in the Uttam Nagar area," Sharad Aggarwal said. They all started the supply of fake notes in Delhi and Kolkata.

Shamim is from Birganj in Nepal. He disclosed that one Motilal there used to get fake notes from Bangladesh. Shamim used to supply these notes to many people in Bihar and at the border in Ruxol.

He used to supply these notes to old parties at their addresses and new parties were being called to Birganj in Nepal, as he knew the Indian police doesn't have jurisdiction in Nepal.

Heading: Top hospitals aspire for air ambulances, rooftop helipads before Commonwealth Games - Indian Express
Content:
Gurgaon's traffic woes might soon become a thing of the past. Urban Mass Transit Company Ltd, engaged by the administration for providing relief from round-the-clock traffic jams, has prepared a plan called the "Integrated Mobility Plan for Gurgaon-Manesar Urban Complex", which was presented on Friday to the officials concerned.

Director, Town and Country Planning, S S Dhillon has asked the officers concerned for suggestions by November 10. The consultant company has prepared a short, medium and long-term draft mobility plan for Gurgaon, which is divided into three phases — first from 2008 to 2011, the second from 2011 to 2017 and the third phase from 2017 to 2021.

"The population of Gurgaon is expected to touch the 43 lakh-mark by 2021, and would increase to 59 lakh by 2031. High volumes of traffic are also expected to pass through because of the Reliance SEZ and other economic zones being developed around the city. On the basis of a survey, the company has laid down the requirements for smoothening the movement of people and cargo," Dhillon said.

The deputy commissioner said three bus stands have also been proposed at Rajiv Chowk, Sector-29 and near Village Panchgaon on NH 8. The company has also proposed eight foot-over bridges on the Expressway.

Heading: Armed robbers tie family up in Preet Vihar, escape with cash, valuables - Indian Express
Content:
Ahead of the Commonwealth Games, the most 'in-thing' that every super specialty hospital seems to want is an air ambulance and a helipad. Most hospitals are banking on the Games to get permission for a helipad adding an unexplored dimension to patient care and emergency services.

While air medical evacuation is already done in most super specialty hospitals in the Capital, having a helipad on the hospital roof is the next big thing. The All India Institute of Medical Sciences applied for permission from the Civil Aviation Ministry last year. Indraprastha Apollo Hospitals is also hoping for permission from authorities before the Games begin. According to sources, with Apollo in line for a helipad, competitors like Escorts, Max and Fortis are not to be left behind.

Max is also looking at helipads for its newer projects, said Dr Parvez Ahmed, Executive Director, Max Healthcare. They are already into end-to-end emergency service. Recently, an Italian was brought in from Chandigarh, treated and the hospital staff accompanied her back home to Milan. "No concrete decisions have been take yet but we are looking at this opportunity for our newer projects," said Dr Ahmed.

The Directorate General of Civil Aviation (DGCA) has issued guidelines for planning, infrastructure, markings and safety regulations for construction of roof-top helipads. "Both hospitals, AIIMS and Apollo, have some internal issues that have to be solved first before they are given permission," said J S Rawat, Joint Secretary, DGCA. Apollo Hospitals had applied for a helipad on the hospital premises five years ago.

"Despite timely air rescues, helipads are the need of the hour as getting to hospital from the airport takes a lot of time, given the traffic snarls in the Capital," said Dr Anupam Sibal, Medical Director, Indraprastha Apollo Hospitals. "Medical care in Delhi is cutting edge and has improved to such a degree that we get many requests for airlifts. The next logical step is to come straight to hospital as in Western countries. This is how emergency care is given the world over and we should look at how we can get to that level," said Dr Sibal. Indraprastha Apollo Hospital has not been given permission yet because it falls in the Delhi air corridor.

Heading: Expat Delhi - Indian Express
Content:
Six armed robbers entered a Preet Vihar house, tied up the family and made away with cash and valuables reportedly amounting to lakhs. Police said the incident took place in the home of one Subodh Jain, a businessman in G-Block, Preet Vihar.

Police said Subodh Jain (42), his wife, Neetu (38) and his mother, Kiran (70) were sleeping on the ground floor in the main bedroom of the house. Kiran is a heart patient.

"Around 3 am, six armed men entered the house through the kitchen and made their way to the bedroom. They tied up all three with their own clothes and gagged them. Then they removed the women's jewellery and looted some cash lying around," a senior policeman said.

Police said robbers fled without untying the residents. They were, however, able to free themselves around 4.30 am. Police said a robbery case has been registered against unknown persons.

Subodh Jain trades in paper in Chawri Bazaar. He has two children, who were away at his sister's house.

Heading: Woman dies in Blueline accident - Indian Express
Content:
Elsa Bernard

A French citizen, Elsa (22) moved to New Delhi in September and works in a small clothes-making unit

* What brings you to India?


My sister travelled a lot around India and told me a great deal about her trips. I really wanted to know more about this country. As far as my job is concerned, it was also very interesting to come to India since it is one of the main exporters of clothes. I was looking forward to discovering Indian handwoven textiles.

* How is it to work with Indian people?
It took me some time to get used to the Indian way of working. For instance, when you set up an appointment, people tend to be late. Plus, in textile production you have to check everything very carefully because the European quality standards are very high when compared to Indian standards.

* A Delhiite's worst habit?
People keep staring at me in the streets. It's kind of disturbing. Even if you're trying to behave like an Indian woman, dressed like an Indian woman, you're always considered a foreigner.

* Do you use public transportation?
Never. I always use autorickshaws because they are very convenient, you don't have to wait for them and they are not crowded.

* Favourite place in Delhi?
Old Delhi, especially Kinari Bazar. Here you can find any kind of accessories, from ribbons to paper crafts. I really like to get lost in the alleys, everything is so colourful and full of life. Another place I love is Lodhi Gardens because it is very peaceful and does not seem to be in the heart of Delhi.

* Favourite food?
Assamese, because it is very healthy and fat-free. I'm a big fan of tea. As for restaurants, I like to go to the Big Chill in Khan Market. There you can have pasta or other European food and they serve amazing chocolate cakes.

* Did you pick up some Indian words or habits?
I'm doing the Indian nod. I eat with my hands and I keep saying "theek hai" or "achcha".

Heading: Swarms of insects keep shoppers at bay - Indian Express
Content:
A Blueline bus claimed yet another life in Paschim Vihar area of West Delhi. Police said the incident was reported at 9.30 on Friday night. Surender Kumar (32) and his wife, Rachna (29) were travelling on a bike, when a speeding Blueline hit them from behind.

The bus was plying on route number 980 (Nangloi to Central Secretariat). The couple was immediately rushed to Sanjay Gandhi Hospital where Rachna was declared dead on arrival. She suffered severe head injuries. Surender's condition is said to be stable in the hospital. He lives in Mauj Vihar.

Heading: Congress outs poll list of 53 - Indian Express
Content:
It's not just the inflation that is keeping shoppers at home. Small insects that cling to lights on the streets and even inside shops are making shopping difficult after sunset.

Some shop owners in popular shopping destinations like Khan Market, Karol Bagh and Rajouri Garden have installed electric pest killers, which have, however, not been very effective. "I have installed one pest killer. But every time the door opens the insects sneak in. It can't be avoided," Kailash Arora, a shop owner in Karol Bagh, said. He said his customers say they prefer to come during the day.

The situation is worse for shops that have open counters. "My shop has no doors. There is no way we can stop the insects from getting in," Subhash Sharma, shop owner in Rajouri Garden, said. Sharma, however, said his sales have not been affected. "I don't think the insects can stop shoppers. Those who have to shop will shop whether insect or no insect," Sharma, a cloth merchant, said.

Shop owners at Khan Market also agree that there is a problem but no solution. "This problem persists all over the city and since it is just a matter of few days, nobody is taking it seriously. All we can do is put off a few lights but then that too is not of much help," shop owner Karanjeet Singh said. Some shops have installed the electric pest killer. "As long as we have enough customers it is not a problem," Singh said.

"We too are witnessing the problem but we know that it is just a matter of few days. Some shops owners have put small traps on the doors under the light to catch the insects," Satendar Wadhwa of Greater Kailash I market, said.

Some shoppers, however, feel undeterred by the insect menace. "There are insects in our homes, in Metro stations — every where. What difference does it makes if they are there in the market place as well?" Preeti Khanna, a shopper at Khan Market, asked."I am aware of the problem and I wanted to come during the day time. I have to complete my shopping before Diwali. So insects don't make a difference," Sneh Chopra, another Shopper, said.

The civic authorities are also aware of the problem. "The MCD carries out routine fogging for mosquitoes. These insects pose no harm and are around for just a few weeks. We do not spray any insecticides to kill them," an MCD official said.

Heading: The Dead and the Alive - Indian Express
Content:
After flitting from one TV show to another, city's Surveen Chawla has taken the big leap into Bollywood

It's heartening to hear her admit at first go, "I am 'wholly and soully' from Chandigarh" the moment we make the introductions over the phone. It's been a while since Surveen Chawla made that visit back home. "Yes, and I am really looking forward to making it in time for Diwali," mentioned the actor who is currently "in step" with Indian cricketer Sreesanth on the dance reality show 'Ek Khiladi, Ek Haseena'. For someone who stepped into Mumbai with absolutely no references to boast, our girl from GCG-11 has come a long way. "Television happened by default. In fact I wasn't making a conscious attempt at a career in acting," reminisces Chawla who walked into a Balaji audition and never looked back. After character roles in shows like 'Kasauti Zindagi Kay' and 'Kahin To Hoga', the petite actor made her presence felt with Sony's primetime show 'Kajjal' where she played the lead role. And then just as her surprise entry, Surveen made a quick exit from tellydom. "Many people thought I was missing in action," laughs Chawla. But all that for a reason. "The offers from Bollywood had begun and I decided to take them up," she admits. But not before she signed up for the dance reality show on Colors.

"I had been approached for a reality show earlier on but I didn't want to do just anything. The concept of 'Ek Khiladi, Ek Haseena' excited me and you know how cricket is a religion in this country," tells Surveen whose pairing with Sreesanth seems perfectly in step. "We share a good chemistry on the floor and I think he can dance really well," is all Chawla is saying at the moment. As for the competition, Surveen is quick to say there's none now in the semi-finals! "I felt Vinod Kambli and Shama Sikander, who are unfortunately out, were really good," she says adding, "Not that the others are not but they could have given tough competition." With the finals not too far, Surveen's got her fingers crossed. And then what? "There is a Kannada and Telegu film in the pipeline. I have also signed a three-film deal with Percept Picture Company. The first is what we are shooting for currently. It's being directed by Chandrakant Kulkarni and I am paired opposite Ranvir Shorey," lists out Surveen who has said her goodbyes to television, for now.

Heading: Swathed in Cause - Indian Express
Content:
Delhiite Rajesh Jala on his Children of the Pyre that has won the best documentary award in Montreal

This is Manikarnika — the busiest cremation ground in India. Here people come with the hope of dying quietly and attaining nirvana. Here, ironically, a clutch of children comes face to face with death everyday. They make a living here, they play games here. Young feet quietly scurry through pyres glinting in the dark and young hands search bodies to steal shrouds. This is where Delhi-based filmmaker Rajesh S. Jala spent days and nights with his camera and those kids, filming the documentary Children of the Pyre.

In the crowded halls of Montreal and Pusan film festivals where Children of the Pyre was screened — at the former, it won the Best Documentary Award — the 74-minute film had a chilling effect from the very first shot. As drum beats pound, orange flames flickering from a pyre fill the dark screen and a shadow scampers across, tightly clutching a shroud. The camera zooms in to disclose the face of 11-year-old Gagan. Dressed in faded clothes, his face deprived of innocence, he is one of Jala's seven protagonists. They are all 9-to-15-year-olds, who sell shrouds stolen from the bodies at Manikarnika. "The seven of them are representatives of several others across India," says Jala, 39.

The filmmaker knows every little detail of the children who were complete strangers until two years ago, when he first visited Varanasi with the intention of making a film in the city. "The place lures filmmakers," smiles Jala, who spent more than a month walking by the ghats and through the narrow lanes. He finally reached Manikarnika to film the life of a widow, but it was the children who caught his attention. "They belong to the Dom community and are considered untouchable. They work here to earn a few rupees and I was convinced that I had to film them," says Jala, who had earlier made the film Floating Lamp of the Shadow Valley about the nine-year-old boatman Arif in his hometown Kashmir.

A few months later, Jala returned to Varanasi with his crew. "We were stationed there 24x7," he says. Even though the inhabitants of Manikarnika were initially unsure of his intentions and conscious of the camera, soon the ice was broken. So, in his narrative he pans from children fighting for shrouds to sell them in the market, to them facing the angry relatives of the dead. In some lighthearted moments, Gagan enjoys a dance with girls during the Navratri festival and Ravi shares details of a romance. However, the humour gives way to dissonance, for even their games revolve around the dead — in one shot, they perform a mock cremation of an abandoned body.

While Jala awaits the premiere here at the International Film Festival of India in Goa in November, before that he travels to Germany for the Leipzig International Film Festival. But there won't be any more films until he establishes a trust to rehabilitate the children of Manikarnika. "I want the kids out of there and in school," says Jala, as he plans another trip to Varanasi — this time to show the children their own tale that has given them recognition worldwide.

Heading: Brushstrokes and Notes - Indian Express
Content:
Designer Krishna Mehta's spring-summer collection realises an old dream — and it is not about clothes

Years ago, fresh out of college and raring to do something for society, designer Krishna Mehta enrolled for a course in training physically and mentally challenged individuals. When she finished the course, one of her teachers had an advice for her. "I was so distraught by their condition that my teacher told me not to get into teaching. She said I could help them only if I treated them as equals," recalls Mehta.

It's an advice that took Mehta some two decades to assimilate. For her spring-summer collection for 2009, the designer has worked with a team of physically challenged and differently abled individuals from a school that she has set up in Palanpur on the Gujarat-Rajasthan border. The school, Palak, takes in differently abled people who have passed high school, and train them in crafts like surface texturisation, dyeing, embroidery and blockprinting. Accordingly, the collection is rich with indigenous handicrafts from across India. "The thought was always there in the back of my mind, but it was only last year that the idea took shape," says Mehta.

The school has about 25 artisans, who have been chosen from about 180 applicants. They have been trained for about eight months and Mehta herself oversees the training. Most of the people who have been employed come from nearby villages and are paid a monthly stipend of Rs 3,000-6,000. The ones who work as managers earn around Rs 10,000. "I have been in the fashion industry for over 25 years now, and it's taken me a long time to get to the point where I can give something back to the community. It is a tiny contribution, but it gives me great satisfaction," she says.

Heading: Zing of Seven Strings - Indian Express
Content:
Sanjoy Ghosh puts his artwork on bottles of wine, but his canvases are not just about heady vintages

You didn't necessarily have to be tipsy to see Picasso on a bottle of wine. You just had to be lucky. Chateau Mouton Rothschild had Picasso, Dali, Warhol and a host of artists design the labels of each year's vintage — the label outside as exhilarating as the fine Bordeaux within. But connoisseurs of Indian wines never had it so rich — until now.

When Manesar-based Vin Opera launches, in a few months, its wine labels Rosso di Montalcino, Brunello di Montalcino, Barbera Piemonte and Amarone della di Valpolicella under its Italian range, the bottle labels will have, arguably for the first time, works by an Indian artist — Kolkata-based Sanjoy Ghosh.

Ghosh's large canvases — a few of which have been subsequently reduced to 4 x 3 inch label format — are on display at the Travancore House. If one has a skeletal figure prancing in a brightly lit house, another has an enlarged face of a woman occupying the skyline of an urban cityscape. "These are the aftereffects of consuming wine," chuckles Ghosh.

The exhibition "The Waiting" is Ghosh's first solo in Delhi. "The title signifies the long wait before art lovers begin to recognise my work," sighs the 50-year-old. The brushstrokes are not just about grapes dreaming in oak barrels. They are intimations of mortality. If Nature and Instinct juxtaposes a human skeleton with a pink bud, The Cycle has a skeleton lying on the ground with strings attached to its ribs and The Quest has two of these figures reaching out to each other.

(The show ends today)

Heading: Last Gasp - Indian Express
Content:
Suit Yourself!

Holland & Sherry, the finest cloth in the world, will be presented to India by Digjam, one of the leading brands in the Indian worsted textile industry. Holland & Sherry, Scotland, is one of the most prestigious cloth weavers in the world and for the last 170 years have been playing a leading role in supplying cloth to the top-end of the market, be it tailors, Parisian haute couture fashion houses and high class garment manufacturers. Now to serve the growing category of elite customers in India, Digjam Limited of the S K Birla Group has tied up with Holland & Sherry to make available rare suiting fabric in the Indian market. The Holland & Sherry Collection will offer 'Escorial' the finest Merino wool, 'Monadh' the world's only authentic Scottish Merino wool, exclusive to Holland & Sherry, 'Snowy River' from the Snowy River Mountain region of Australia.

Sparkle & Shine

The Diwali celebration of Swami Vivekanand Groups of Institutes lived up to its theme 'Sparkle 2008'. Here while the students put up a great show of cultural extravaganza, they were also asked to prepare a balance sheet of their knowledge gained every academic year, by the chief guest NC Jain, Field General Manager, PNB, Chandigarh. The highlight of the programme was a resolution made by the students to undertake a series of programmes regarding eradication of social menaces like female feticide, dowry greed, forcible marriages and illiteracy of the girl child.

Get Global

How often do 800 students from all across the city come together to discuss and learn more about the current global issues concerning us? Hardly ever! Providing platform is AIESEC, which is conducting the Learning Networks Day on October 30 at St Stephen's School, Sector 45 B from 10 am to 2 pm with an aim to broaden perspectives about global issues. The event would have sessions by experts and team activities facilitated by AIESEC's international interns. These sessions would be on issues like HIV/AIDS, entrepreneurship, technological divide and traffic awareness. Learning Networks Day would also be a great platform for like-minded youth to network amongst each other and share perspectives on social as well as managerial issues of the world. AIESEC will also launch its new initiative, Youth Volunteer Enterprise (You'Ve), where in the members will encourage youth volunteerism and provide an issue based experience. The registration can be done online at www.aiesecchandigarh.org

Curtain Call

After GM and DC -TEX, Curtain House has now started keeping Kurlon mattress too. A place known for a vast variety of curtains, bed covers and blankets, "here you will be spoilt for choice," says Sanjay Chopra, proprietor of the store.

Home in!

Mapping the real estate market is Zirakpur. With builders, estaters and colonizers eyeing it because of its geographical location and significant developmental prospects, besides its USP of about 54 per cent greenery, Maya Estatz is the amongst the first ones to spot the opportunity. Using its rich experience in residential building and state-of-art technology, the man behind the endeavour Satish Jindal, MD, Barnala Builders & Property Consultants, tell us, "With more than 30 years of expertise in the field of real estate and service sector and Goldmine Complex and Silver Enclave as the living examples, in Maya Garden Apartments, we will add nuances that will make living comfortable." Maya Garden has 291 flats and promises earthquake resistant buildings and RCC frame structure. The floorings, they tell us differ from room to room according to requirements of décor and convenience. "Living rooms have vitrified tiles with skirting and bed rooms are provided with laminated wooden flooring. Modular kitchens are spacious with antiskid ceramic tiles," reels Jindal. With the wall finishes worth a dekko, here they assure all amenities which a modern home demands. For more, a visit to Maya Garden Apartment will tell you all.

Heading: Tales from Cusrow Baug - Indian Express
Content: The Lakme Fashion Week drew to a close on Friday. On a day when bad designs reigned supreme, Anuj Sharma emerged a winner with his "Knot for You" collection. The collection revolved around strategically placed knots that bound, shaped, draped and constructed his carefully tailored outfits. Effortlessly chic, he only made use of crepe and georgette. For a Grecian effect, the designer knotted the fabric to create versions of flowers or a butterfly-like effect and held the garments at the shoulders with the help of slim black ribbons. Meanwhile, the ensemble of the day went to Aneeth and Chinar of Gaba, who created some rustic magic with their khadi and handloom line. What we loved the most was a pair of loose pedal pushers in white teamed with a two-layered, smock, flowing green tunic with a white embroidered gamcha thrown around the bag. Nice. But thank god, the fashion weak is over.

Heading: The sandwich age - Indian Express
Content:
A peek into the Parsi bastion in Colaba, which is out of bounds for most Mumbaikars

On Colaba Causeway, there is a place that intrigues the non-Parsis a lot. For over six years, we've have gone up and down the Causeway a million times, each time thinking about what goes on within the fortress called Cusrow Baug. A lovely residential sanctuary, the Baug situated across the road from Café Churchill is also a gateway to traditional Parsi ways of life and culture.

Cusrow Baug was built in 1934 after two years of construction. In present day Mumbai, it may seem totally unbelievable, but the Baug covers an area of 84,000 square yards and is home to over 500 families. The houses are all on a rental basis and cannot be sold.

There is a designated trust looking after maintenance of the place. This ensures that the place remains exclusive to the community.

A dedicated website called cusrowbaug.org tells us that self-contained as it is, the Baug has an Agiary named The Seth Nusserwanji Hirji Karani Agiary. It also has a social activities cell which carries out educational initiatives, including religion classes and some scholarships. The Religious Class in the baug is one of the most valuable and dedicated service of the colony to the Parsi community. This is credited to a few dedicated people who have carried out social service for the past 22 years. There is also a full-fledged sports centre called Cusrow Baug United Sports and Welfare League. They have a computer centre and a gymnasium too. However, this website hasn't been updated since 2004.

For the Parsis, the dwindling numbers of the community is quite a huge concern. Even at Cusrow Baug there aren't many young people around. No wonder then that it is no less than a festival for them when neighbours fall in love and get married to stay in the Baug forever.

Cusrow Baug remains a place surrounded by mysterious charm. For its residents, it is the best place on earth. For most of us, this haven is out of bounds.

Heading: Space prop for more low-income housing - Indian Express
Content:
Too young to report crime, but too old to while away time in a café

In April, I became a graduate, finally. I don't think I grabbed the implications of that then. But it meant that life had changed. There'd been changes before. After studying in four schools and two colleges, I was no stranger to change.

Having always been the puny one at school, I was used to being treated like the youngest one in the class. But I had pretty much got used to enjoying my seniority at college, what with being a contingent leader and managing my college's cultural fests. Also when I could spare time I started working for a student organisation called AIESEC and was a team leader. Nothing can give a bigger kick than walking into a corporate office to represent this organisation and negotiate the details of an MoU.

When I became a graduate, I felt like I was more qualified then most of my friends. So when I got into the professional world, there no guarding or warning me against the fact that I was a rookie. Because that's what I was.

Here, I was the only one in my peer group with a job I wanted. Unlike them, I wouldn't crib about thankless hours spent in front of a computer and no meaningful or fun work to do since a job description rarely comes cooler than 'crime reporter'. There I was on top again.

But things couldn't be further from the truth at office. I soon realised that my years in college had filled me with some sort of a complex that I was somehow better than most. The truth came crashing down to me in my first week as I struggled to get stories and bylines. When I was rushing to police stations looking for the details of the latest murder, I could read the look in the officer's eyes: "They get younger every year." Once an officer even blurted, "You are very young. How old really are you?".

In fact in a certain press conference of doctors, someone actually asked the PR guys, "Is he really a reporter? He looks like a child." Pretending that I had not heard the whispers, I soldiered on. But the hammer really fell when my

Editor-in-Chief looked at me and said "It looks like someone's brought his nephew to office."

However, among my friends I am still the oldest. They take weekend off to go to Goa, bunk college and lounge in a café and infuriate me with successive messages asking me to be with them in the afternoons when I work. The days I manage to go out to catch up them, I'm the late guy because of work. All's fine till the pretty girl you were talking to suddenly asks which college you belong to. Her surprise that I work is followed by the incredulous "How old are you?".

So it seems I'm too young to work and too old to party. Harsh, isn't it? I don't know if I should crawl into some working class bar or head to the latest trendy nightspot.

(adityampaul@gmail.com)

Heading: BEST hopes ordinance will make MNS pay - Indian Express
Content:
The Maharashtra Area and Housing Development Authority (MHADA) has a plan up its sleeve that may improve the city skyline, which is now characterised by swanky skyscrapers flanked by vast stretches of slums.

The move, once approved by the government, will pave the way for more Low Income Group homes.

MHADA's integrated housing proposal for Mumbai suggests that all development and redevelopment projects in the city be allowed more buildable area by way of extra Floor Space Index (FSI) — if they include homes for Low Income Groups (LIG) in their project.

According to MHADA vice-president Gautam Chatterjee, it will be a joint venture between MHADA which will grant the FSI, while the private developer will bring in the land. The technology and infrastructure too will be through joint efforts.

"Even if MHADA is to go for the project on its own, it will anyway have to purchase land at market rates. MHADA will oversee the adequacy of infrastructure and quality of construction through a Project Management Consultant or on its own. Once construction is complete, the LIG houses will be sold by MHADA while the MIG and HIG (High Income Group) homes will sold by the private developers," said Chatterjee.

The proposal is based on the housing policy which mentions that all private layouts should have mandatory zoning provisions for LIG housing. The policy also talks about giving incentives for construction of LIG tenements.

State housing secretary Sitaram Kunte said the proposed FSI for such joint ventures would be 2.5.

"The proposal is pending with the Urban Development department," he said.

MHADA sources added that while the housing policy mentions the proportion for LIG, MIG, and HIG as 10:10: 80 respectively, MHADA plans to increase the LIG share. MHADA has proposed that the policy be implemented not only in the Mumbai Metropolitan Region but for all A class municipal corporations, as well as for any development in an area within 10 km of their periphery. "This is taking into consideration rapid urbanisation of these cities," said Chatterjee.

He added that the sale of LIG flats will be done through the proper selection system and MHADA's lottery system.

Heading: Thanks to NGOs, families of 2 cops dead in riots to have better Diwali - Indian Express
Content:
Damage during MNS agitations estimated at around Rs 72 lakh

Everytime Raj Thackeray's Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS) takes to the streets to bat for Maharashtrians, Mumbai's road transport lifeline, the iconic BEST buses, suffer the maximum damage.

And now, BEST is pinning its hope on a state government ordinance to recover the losses suffered during the agitations by various political parties, the MNS in particular.

The estimated loss to the city's public transport during the MNS agitations stands at around Rs 72 lakh, with 264 buses damaged and 22 drivers, four conductors and four passengers injured. The maximum damage caused was allegedly during the MNS agitations in February and October with nearly 98 per cent of the total loss because of stone-pelting.

Since January, the city witnessed eight tumultuous days. There was stone-pelting, raasta rokos and bandhs on these days. Notable ones were the agitation following the death of a Buddhist priest, the MNS agitation against north Indians, stir by Sikhs over the issue of firing by a bodyguard of Baba Ram Rahim in Mulund, bandh over the Amarnath land transfer row and the most recent MNS agitation against north Indians.

The estimate is that the maximum damage was caused during three days of the MNS agitation, two days in February when there were talks of Raj's imminent arrest before he was actually arrested and released on bail and then on October 21, when the MNS chief was arrested yet again.

During the MNS agitations, bus services were cancelled in many routes and rescheduled in many others to ensure commuters' safety. However, despite the precautions, several drivers, conductors and citizens were injured.

General Manager, BEST, Uttam Khobragade, said the transport undertaking would think of recovering the costs once the ordinance cleared by the cabinet on Wednesday comes into force. "If the law allows us to recover the money from MNS, we will definitely do it," he said.

MNS, on the other hand, does not seem keen to pay up. "It has not been proved that the damage to BEST was done by MNS activists. If it is proved then we will see," said MNS spokesperson, Nitin Sardesai.

Heading: Traders move court against proposed skywalk at Grant Road in Dadar - Indian Express
Content:
Organisations have been instrumental in helping two houses after Thane police constables were lynched by mob during 2006 Bhiwandi riots

For Manisha Gangurde, this year's Diwali is special. For nearly two years after her father's death, she has lit up a lantern and made a rangoli outside her house in Vartak Nagar in Thane. It's a similar story at the Jagtap family's house in Police Lines colony near the Thane police commissioner's office.

The two homes lost their heads of their families, Ramesh Jagtap and Balu Gangurde, both constables with the Thane Police, in July 2006 when they were lynched by a mob during the Bhiwandi riots.

The two families are set to have a colourful Diwali this year courtesy Pune-based NGO, Bhoi Pratishthan, and a group of youngsters from the Rashtrabhakt Yuva Manch (RYM).

The NGO and the RYM members provided the families with sweets, rangoli, lantern and firecrackers as a moral support. "We want them to know that some one is there behind them," says Dr Milind Bhoi, founder-president of the NGO and an ENT specialist.

The initiative to make these two families' Diwali colourful is the brainchild of the RYM. The group, every year, spends the day of Diwali with the families of the braves who laid down their life for the country. It also arranges for the cultural programmes for the postmen, class-four employees of the Pune Municipal Corporation. "If these people can lay down their lives for us, this is a small effort from our side to make them happy," says Vaibhav Wagh, president of the youth group and an event manager.

After losing head of their families, both the household were going through trying times. The Gangurde family had a daughter of marriageable age, and another daughter and a teenaged son to educate. Similarly, the Jagtap family had a boy and two daughters— all school-going when the incident occurred. At that time, the families were adopted by the Bhoi Pratishthan. The help kept on coming at regular intervals.

The NGO, soon after the death of the two policemen, donated Rs 1 lakh to the families. Last year, Gangurde's daughter Poonam got married and a substantial help came from the NGO. "They prepared the mangalsutra for our sister and also provided household items like utensils for the marriage," says Manisha, Balu Gangurde's daughter, who is doing her diploma course and wants to be a teacher. Her younger brother is studying in grade XII. "Apart from financial support, their moral support was always there behind us, which mattered a lot," says Ramesh Jagtap (15), a class IX student.

Making a difference

Bhoi Pratishthan: Has adopted Helwas, a displaced village in the Koyna river valley; various programmes for children who polish shoes at the railway station and holds health check-up for policemen

Rashtrabhakt Yuva Manch: Mobilises college youth for social work; runs a helpline for blind students and has a prepared database of 50,000 blood donors who can be approached at the time of crisis

Say not against city's growth but misuse of public revenue

The Federation of Retail Traders Welfare Association and others have moved the Bombay High Court challenging the proposed skywalks at Grant Road and Dadar.

As per the petition, these two proposed skywalks are: one between Grant Road station and Nana Chowk circle, and another between Ranade Road and M C Jawale Marg in Dadar.

The petitioners states that the Grant Road (West) Retail Traders Association and Dadar Merchants Association have complained to them and they have shown strong objection to the proposed skywalk. They state that they are not against the growth of the city but against the misuse of public revenue as more than Rs 600 crore of public money is going to be used for 54 skywalks across the city.

The petitioners further say that if the skywalk is made only for the pedestrians and there is enough width of the road and there is no objection from the local residents and shopkeepers then the association has no objection. Heading: Fake shoes get the boot - Indian Express
Content:
Bollywood can play a role in cancer awareness, says Chief of Protocol, US State Department

The world can learn from India what a family can do to help breast cancer patients. This was the observation of the Chief of Protocol, US State Department, Nancy Brinker. She said India can teach the world how families, by giving emotional support, can play an important role in curing the second most common cancer in women across the world.

Brinker, who was attending the 6th Tata Memorial Hospital Women's Cancer Initiative Conference on Saturday, said she was touched by the way families in India are involved in treatment modules for the patient. She added that the emotional support for the patients seen in India was not so common in the US.

Brinker, who is here to learn from the clinical experience of Indian doctors and researchers, also said Bollywood films could be used as a tool to spread awareness on breast cancer and boost the confidence of patients.

A cancer patient herself, Brinker is the founder of the Susan Komen for the Cure, named after her only sister, Susan, who died of the disease in 1980. The foundation is today recognised as a leading catalyst in the fight against breast cancer in the US.

The Tata Memorial Hospital has taken up a large clinical breast-testing programme on 150,000 women residing in slums of Mumbai, in addition to women in Ratnagiri and Sindhudurg districts of Maharashtra.

"The study began in 1997 where girls in 20 slum areas across the city were trained for Clinical Breast Examination (CBE). They went to the community and clinically examined women and repeated it every two years. So far, four rounds of screening have been completed and the programme has been able to detect 87 per cent of expected breast cancer cases and 81 per cent of expected cervix cancer cases," said Dr S Shastri, professor and head, department of preventive oncology.

The hospital will be coming out with efficacy of the method by November-end.

In India, breast cancer sets in almost a decade early as compared to the US. "Mean age at detection of breast cancer in western countries is 58 years, that is after menopause, whereas in India, it is 49 years. Almost 10 years younger women are predisposed to breast cancer in India," said Dr S Shastri, head of preventive oncology department, at the conference.

That's also partly the reason for the high mortality rate in India, because women are not screened early or the disease is not detected early using mammography. "Mammography is not as effective in developing countries like India for detection of breast cancer, because any breast abnormality is difficult to detect in pre-menopausal women. Besides, the cost and availability is an issue," said Shastri.

In her keynote address "Breast Cancer Alleviation", Brinker said the Indian government should set up a lot of regional cancer centres so that people in remote areas can avail themselves of the facilities at the nearest location. "This is important as the crisis of cancer is being ignored even by the United Nation's Millennium programme and other international health institutions," she said.

Asked whether people of America are opting for alternate therapies, she said, "Yes, a lot of oncologists are combining complementary therapy."

Heading: Short-circuit caused Laxmi Industrial Estate fire - Indian Express

Shops raided, counterfeit Nike, Adidas shoes seized, six arrested based on an information given by city firm

In a crackdown on footwear shops pushing fakes in the market using using logos of popular brands, Kurla police arrested six persons and confiscated 449 pairs of shoes carrying fake Nike and Adidas logos.

The police raided four shops on Friday acting on information given by a firm, Rose India Pvt Ltd.

"Rose India Pvt Ltd has an agreement with Adidas and Nike whereby it tracks copyright violations. It's the company's task to identify individuals or agencies selling duplicate goods using Nike or Adidas brands. The company representatives, upon finding them, gather evidence and initiate criminal proceedings. Kshitij Akluskar, the West Zone manager of Rose India complained that four shops in Kurla were selling fake Adidas and Nike shoes," said Kurla Police Inspector (Crime), B Jadhav.

A police team from Kurla accompanied Akluskar to the shops and raided them. All the shoes bearing the logos were confiscated. "On a tip-off that the shopowners had more stock in some godown in Pydhonie, we reached the place, but found it closed," Jadhav said.

The arrested were identified as Prakash Ahire, Taufiq R Shaikh, Mohammed Javed Sheikh, Mohammed Irfan Sheikh, Sheikh Mohammed and Malang Mehmood Sheikh. They have ben charged under the Copyright Act and section 420 of the Indian Penal Code relating to cheating.

"The value of the seized goods is approximately Rs 12.33 lakh. No doubt, the goods are fake. Rose India made the estimate of the fakes keeping cost of the originals in mind," said Police sub-inspector R D Vichare, who is investigating the case.

The police will send samples of the seized lot to Adidas and Nike companies for verification. "We will also move an application in court seeking permission to dispose of the seized goods," said Jadhav.

Heading: New releases - Indian Express
Content:
The fire that gutted the interiors of a soon-to-be-opened restaurant at Laxmi Industrial Estate on Friday was caused by a short-circuit in some wires. The restaurant consisted of four galas (small areas) that were connected plus a fifth gala, which the restaurant management told the fire brigade officials, was planned to be a kitchen area.

The fire follows on the heels of a similar fire this month in another industrial estate in Oshiwara. The industrial estates came under the scanner of the Mumbai Fire Brigade after the Retiwala Industrial Estate fire incident in which 10 people had died. The fire brigade then found out that almost all of these estates flouted fire-safety regulations. However, since the fire brigade has no punitive or enforcing powers, they find that their hands are tied.

"What can we do? We can't deny fighting a fire because someone has flouted safety norms, can we? It is up to the BMC ward officers to enforce our suggestions and take action," said S A Mahdi, Divisional Fire Officer.

About the latest case, the DFO said: "While the industrial estate did have a water tower as required, we had to use one of the neighboring buildings as the tower was too far to be of use. The galas, however, had no fire exits and were clearly flouting rules." Mahdi added, "Owners should be more aware of fire safety to prevent such incidents."

Heading: Mhatre wins markers snooker title - Indian Express
Content:
Oh so cool

Roadside Romeo

Indian animation has finally come of age. Roadside Romeo, the first Walt Disney-Yash Raj roll-out is a barrel of fun: bole toh, ekdum jhakaas, baap.

It combines the best aspects of both studios—Disney's expertise in creating animated figures which live and breathe, and Yash Raj's forte in frothy romance: What better than getting Romeo and Laila voiced by real-life lovers Saif ali Khan and Kareena Kapoor?

Romeo is a one-time pampered pooch, now abandoned on the mean streets of Mumbai. Laila is a saucy, red-scarf-around-her-dainty-neck dancer, who only has to bat her impossibly large eyelashes for Romeo to start panting. Trouble looms in the shape of the pug-ugly Charlie Anna (Jaaved Jaaferi), who rules with a ruthless paw, and a bunch of louts. He fancies Laila, and woe is any Tom, Dick, or Romeo who comes in between.

The alacrity with which the characters break into song-and-dance shows that Disney or no Disney, Bollywood rules. Whether style-bhai Romeo is kicking up his heels with his canine pals, or looking for a likely spot to pee ("Yahaan koi toilet nahin hai kya? Man, what a dump") you can actually see Saif, who does cool like no else. And when sexy Laila shakes her charming rump, breathily coming on to her besotted beau, you know that's Kareena. Both sizzle up the screen.

Where debutant director Jugal Hansraj falters is with the villainous Chaaaarrrlie Anna: Jaaferi is made to growl incomprehensibly and break wind more often than getting a chance at being a riot. He does make you guffaw, but only once in a while, and for someone of Jaaferi's goofy brilliance, that's not enough.

But we can live with this Charlie. In his words, he's our chappie, so he makes us happy. We can also handle the strong resemblance our Mumbai-curs have to Disney-style American doggie-doos, because we know that given a chance, they will open their mouths to utter a desi 'bhow bhow' rather than the westernised 'bow wow'. Roadside Romeo is Hindi cinema's first stylish, slick animated feature, which pulls off the toughest feat - appealing to both adults and children.

That's, like, cool, dude.

Lost glory

Heroes

Two city slickers set out to deliver letters from dead servicemen to their far-flung families, and in the process, discover themselves.

The premise of Heroes is interesting. And in parts Samir Karnik's film does manage to say what it set out to: That pride (the Hindi garv is a better word) keeps the families of the deceased soldiers going, that we civilians sleep peacefully only because someone has given up their life for us, and that we have a country only because we have a brave fauji guarding our borders. But the director falls for the easiest trick in the book: He wrings tears out of so many situations that everything-even the supreme sacrifice that the soldiers make-turns trite.

Heroes needed a radical change in treatment, but it falls half-way between keeping things low-key, and going full-tilt at melodrama. What can you do if pretty Preity Zinta is a war-widow, speaking flawless Punjabi, keeping it together for her old in-laws, and a young son? And Salman Khan, her bluff Jat heartthrob, who says: Teri liye lakh jawani, par yeh jawani desh ke naam, or words to that effect. Sunny Deol plays a rum-swilling disabled airman who loses younger brother Bobby Deol, who carried a torch for the Army. Mithun Chakraborty is an embittered father, who hasn't forgiven son Dino Morea for dying. And the two boys-who-turn-into-men on their road journey, armed with a camera and alarming naivete, are Sohail Khan and Vatsal Sheth.

The subject deserved a better film.

SHUBHRA GUPTA

French correction

Days of Glory

Liberte, Egalite, Fraternite. This film examines the three pillars on which the French Republic stands through the eyes of soldiers summoned from its colonies to fight a war for liberalising a people, while enjoying few of those rights themselves.

Put into the worst of battles towards the end of World War II, with the least compensation in terms of money, promotion, leave or even rationed tomatoes, the soldiers from France's colonies in North Africa—particularly Algeria—fight a cold, brutal war and die an unknown death. The government they are fighting for feels no need to even begin understanding their religion, needs or culture.

In a great scene, after one hard-fought battle, the tired African soldiers are offered a "treat": a ballet in a torn tent. Uncomprehending and disgusted, they walk out.

Nominated for the Best Foreign Language Film at the 2007 Oscars and the Golden Palm at Cannes, Days of Glory has some exceptional performances by its lead actors, who have enlisted for the war for their own reasons. There is the scholarly and brave Corporal Abdelkadar (Samy Bouajila), who clings to the belief till the last that the fight against Hitler is his fight; Said (Jamel Debbouze), who finds a reason and hope in his life, led till then in utter poverty, in a place he realises has none of it; Messaoud (Roschdy Zem), who discovers love in the unlikeliest of places; and Sergeant Martinez (Bernard Blancan), a Frenchman in Algeria who is part African, a secret he takes to his grave, constantly torn between the men he knows are being mistreated and his bosses who couldn't care less.

Defeating the Axis powers in Italy, when the Algerian infantry marches into France, it is the first time they have set foot on, what they have been told, is their "motherland". The message is reinforced through martial songs, on speeches, and exhortations to march to yet another battle.

From a small dusty village in Algeria, illiterate and swept up in all that's happening around him, Said has figured it out for himself more clearly. Describing a battle scene, he says: "I threw a bomb at Germany, I beat Germany, all of Germany… I free a country, it is my country. Even if I haven't seen it before."

At the time, he is staring into the eyes of a woman hanging on to his every word, willing to believe anything the soldier of a winning army has to say. The words, you realise, are not for her. Before he marches into certain death, it's Said's prayer, for himself.

SHALINI LANGER
