After reaching home, it is a quick dinner with family before the lights go off. "Hobbies are no longer a part of my life. My family worries because once I get married my personal life will also be more demanding."

Heading: Reel Run - Indian Express
Content:
It's not high stakes, but camaraderie that's on the cards at a Diwali bash

Sometimes honey, it's not only about the money! While playing cards may be an integral and 'auspicious' part of most pre-Diwali bashes, the party's true essence is celebrating the festivity and joy with friends. Laughter, chatter, good food, games...every night is a celebration of fun and friendship. A tradition is how most choose to call their parties, a must-do, year after year.

Diwali is a time to reconnect, let your hair down and be in the company of people you love, smiles Rachna Mehra, who runs a coaching centre and makes sure each Diwali get-together is an affair to remember. "We always say that if you play cards, you invite Laxmi to your home. So for us, it's all about having a carefree time together and not winning or losing, the idea being to be together in this festive mood," the 12-15 of them set aside a kitty after every round for food and drinks, so that it all can ordered and no one has to cook. "There's nothing flashy or formal about the bash and the party just gets better with time," adds the lady.

"Cards are only an excuse to meet up,'' Jaideep Sekhon, a company executive makes sure the plan is in place two weeks before Diwali and at least, three hours starting 9 pm are reserved for the group. Many in Sekhon's close-knit group don't play cards, but are always there for company. This, smiles Jaideep, is the time of the year when people are relaxed, don't feel guilty about eating, sleeping late and simply relaxing. "And it's such a great way to catch up on lost time and play on really small stakes, mostly calling in for food we all like," says Sekhon.

For more than 25 years, Preeti Gill and her comrades have been celebrating Diwali parties almost like a ritual, taking turns to hold the 'event', which everyone awaits every year. "It's a tradition that even our children are carrying forward now," Preeti says the parties are absolute mast affairs, with each one of them taking turns to host the party and cook a feast. "We have many non-playing friends, who make sure they cheer their favourite players,'' Gill adds a surprise and fun element to every party .

Supriya Singh, a banker, soon after Dusshera has afternoon parties every weekend and the venue remains her home. A potluck is what this gang of girls organizes and after the chatting session is over, there are games to be played and prizes to be won. " We make sure we dress up, catch up for at least, three hours and play two serious games of flash and whoever wins the maximum has to treat too! "We just ask for chocolates," smiles Supriya.

Card sessions before Diwali is like a ceremony, which Akhil Bhanot, a property consultant and his friends have been attending since they were together in college, with many friends joining in for festivities from other cities! Many in the group have been together since school and this is the moment they bond and go down memory lane. "What's more, our wives and children have formed their own bonds and it's a huge family affair, one that lasts for more than four hours daily, some two weeks before the festival and we keep shifting venues, ordering or dishing out new cuisines," Akhil gets ready to play!

Heading: Girl on the go! - Indian Express
Content:
It sure is a poster moment especially for collectors and Bollywood buffs who've been on the prowl for years, trying to get their hands on it. People for Animals, Chandigarh, in yet another interesting exhibition-cum-sale are going to pin-up the best of Bollywood's classic collection of posters. "We are constructing our fourth hospital, and could certainly do with more funds!" PFA's Payal Sodhi gives us a lowdown on a series of fund raisers that are being organized on a regular basis. "We've had exhibitions and sale of pottery, oleographs of Raja Ravi Verma , century old lithographs, paintings of Manu Parekh, antique tiles, and now this, film posters titled Divas Unveiled." According to Payal, posters of old classic films is now becoming an art collector's item and is gaining a lot of popularity in the international market. "These posters are also being auctioned by India's reputed auction houses based in Delhi and Mumbai and are rage in the European market, especially those of Amitabh Bachchan's films and Raj Kapoor's," tells Payal, adding how one poster can go for as high as Rs 35,000. "But here we are pricing them between Rs 1,500 and Rs 8,000." The exhibition will include posters of films falling between 1940 and 2007. The posters are first edition prints and are available in two sizes i.e. 40" x 30" & 30"x 20". "Aah, Barsaat, Aan, Boot Polish, Sangam, Shri 420, Mother India, Mugal-e-Azam, Anarkali, Aar Paar, Kati Patang, Khandaan, Do Ankhen Barah Haath, Daag, Johnny Mera Naam, the entire Big B series, latest films like Don (new), Om Shanti Om, Mangal Pandey, Chak de India, Devdas....they are all on display," informs Payal.

This exhibition and sale will be held at the Government Arts Gallery, Sector 10, Chandigarh from the October 31 to November 3. It will remain open from 10 am to 6 pm.

Heading: Colour me wild - Indian Express
Content:
Rajesh Jala on his Children of the Pyre that has won the best documentary award in Montreal

This is Manikarnika — the busiest cremation ground in India. Here people come with the hope of dying quietly and attaining nirvana. Here, ironically, a clutch of children comes face to face with death everyday. They make a living here, they play games here. Young feet quietly scurry through pyres glinting in the dark and young hands search bodies to steal shrouds. This is where Delhi-based filmmaker Rajesh S. Jala spent days and nights with his camera and those kids, filming the documentary Children of the Pyre.

In the crowded halls of Montreal and Pusan film festivals where Children of the Pyre was screened — at the former, it won the Best Documentary Award — the 74-minute film had a chilling effect from the very first shot. As drum beats pound, orange flames flickering from a pyre fill the dark screen and a shadow scampers across, tightly clutching a shroud. The camera zooms in to disclose the face of 11-year-old Gagan. Dressed in faded clothes, his face deprived of innocence, he is one of Jala's seven protagonists. They are all 9-to-15-year-olds, who sell shrouds stolen from the bodies at Manikarnika. "The seven of them are representatives of several others across India," says Jala, 39.

The filmmaker knows every little detail of the children who were complete strangers until two years ago, when he first visited Varanasi with the intention of making a film in the city. "The place lures filmmakers," smiles Jala, who spent more than a month walking by the ghats and through the narrow lanes. He finally reached Manikarnika to film the life of a widow, but it was the children who caught his attention. "They belong to the Dom community and are considered untouchable. They work here to earn a few rupees and I was convinced that I had to film them," says Jala, who had earlier made the film Floating Lamp of the Shadow Valley about the nine-year-old boatman Arif in his hometown Kashmir.

A few months later, Jala returned to Varanasi with his crew. "We were stationed there 24x7," he says. Even though the inhabitants of Manikarnika were initially unsure of his intentions and conscious of the camera, soon the ice was broken. So, in his narrative he pans from children fighting for shrouds to sell them in the market, to them facing the angry relatives of the dead. In some lighthearted moments, Gagan enjoys a dance with girls during the Navratri festival and Ravi shares details of a romance. However, the humour gives way to dissonance, for even their games revolve around the dead — in one shot, they perform a mock cremation of an abandoned body.

While Jala awaits the premiere here at the International Film Festival of India in Goa in November, before that he travels to Germany for the Leipzig International Film Festival. But there won't be any more films until he establishes a trust to rehabilitate the children of Manikarnika. "I want the kids out of there and in school," says Jala, as he plans another trip to Varanasi — this time to show the children their own tale that has given them recognition worldwide.

Heading: Tube talk - Indian Express
Content:
When it comes to Amber, no two pieces are alike!

Before I begin this week's journey, I would like to take a walk down history lane. There was a Roman Emperor Nero who once sent a knight to bring hundreds of pounds of what they called 'Gold of the north' as it matched his wife's hair and enhanced her eyes. The warmth of the golden pebbles that stirred Nero's soul was Amber. Staggering variety of colours, variations in translucency plus that no two natural pieces are alike contribute to its appeal. Named after Ambres, the Celtic Sun God, amber is available in mostly golden hues. It's a vascular tissue of tree that exudes during radical climate change or injury. This vegetative origin gem has the singular ability to encapsulate anything, mostly pieces of flora and fauna it comes in contact with. This 'Time Capsule' has helped the world's scientific community in morphological analysis and identifying nearly 214 plant specimen and 1,000 extinct insect species. It is the softest and lightest in weight of all gems. Amber occurs in over 256 identified shades from nearly black brown, red, green, orange, yellow, cream, white and rarely in blue and violet. Amber stores static electricity. One may rub amber and see how it removes lint from clothes.

Amber has been historically associated with its preservative, healing and symbolic properties. Egyptians revered it as the vessel of eternal youth probably owing to its desiccant properties and is found in their tombs like Tutankhamen's Tomb. Lithunians called it their 'Sunshine Stone' and used an amber neck piece to protect their kids. Latvians exchanged wedding bands in amber to ensure eternal bond. Chinese displayed their wealth by burning huge chunks of amber that exudes a pleasant resinous fragrance and aromatic smoke. Amber incense was also burned in churches. Various cultures esteem amber as a stress buster and in providing mental clarity. Today, it is a much-admired gem by jewellery lovers world over.

Scientific evidence reveals the oldest amber to be originally from Carbon time and is 345 million years old. Amber is found in all continents barring the pole regions. Today most of it is sourced from the Baltic region (finest and rarest) and the Dominican Republic (natural varied colours and blue). Fakes are aplenty in the market and one must be careful. Amber is warm against the skin. True Amber is light enough to float in soft water like soap suds would i.e, not to the top. Pick one that brings out your eyes. Happy hunting!

(The writer is a city-based researcher specialising in jewellery art and can be contacted at sameeraahaan02@gmail.com)

Heading: Big Apple - Indian Express
Content:
Chang Can!

If Mini Mathur and Hussain were the perfect hosts and set the stage on fire last year, Chang and Deepali continued it as the young hosts of Indian Idol 4 auditions this year. Now with the end of theatre round and the start of piano round, viewers got to see Meiyang Chang palying host again! By popular public demand Chang will co-host Indian Idol 4 with Hussain. For the first time ever Indian Idol will has two male hosts. There's no doubt Hussain is a hot favourite and popular with the masses and with Chang's mesmerizing face, dimpled smile and voice we are sure this duo, together will win over the hearts of the audiences across the globe.

Heading: ‘Indian economy to be world’s second largest by 2050’ - Indian Express
Content:
As a special for the festive season, Apple has introduced a new range of iPods. You can take your pick from a wide range of products to fit every pocket ranging from the 1GB iPod shuffle starting at Rs 2,300 to a 32 GB iPod touch at Rs 21,100. With an all-new design, and an amazing set of new features, the world's most popular music player is now available in eight vibrant colours such as silver, purple, blue, green, orange, yellow, pink, and black. The new fourth generation iPod Nano sports a curved aluminum enclosure that feels great in your hand, while the large, 2-inch display makes it easy to enjoy movies, and games. With a choice of models, both 8GB and 16GB you may never want to put the iPod nano down. The new Genius feature turns iPod Nano into your own highly intelligent, personal DJ. It creates playlists by finding songs in your library that go great together. Then there's the iPod Touch which is smaller and lighter and features a thin contoured metal design, a 3.5-inch widescreen glass display, 802.11 b/g Wi-Fi wireless networking, integrated volume control buttons, a built-in speaker for casual listening, a built-in accelerometer and other advanced sensors, and Apple's 'Multi-Touch' user interface. If you are pockets aren't too deep, then there's the iPod Classic and the iPod Shuffle to choose from. With up to 36 hours of audio playback time and a 2.5-inch colour display the iPod Classic is available in quintessential silver or striking new black. The iPod Shuffle priced at 1GB for Rs 2,300 (local taxes apply) and 2GB for Rs 3,200 (local taxes apply) is now available in four vibrant colours blue, green, pink and original silver. Wear up to 500 songs on your sleeve or belt or gym shorts. With the built-in clip, iPod shuffle goes with anything.

All in one

Nokie Nseries, the premium multimedia sub-brand of Nokia, has launched the Nokia N85 in India. The dual-slider Nokia N85 boasts of a vivid 2.6" OLED screen with a super-sleek finish, which redefines the mobile experience and makes it an ideal backdrop for games, images and web-browsing. It comes pre-loaded with 15 try-and-buy made-for-mobile N-Gage games and a voucher for one full game license. Dedicated gaming keys of the device light up when it is in gaming mode to further enhance the action-packed experience. The Nokia N85 will be retailed at an MRP of Rs 27299. "The Nokia N85 was created to be more than the sum of its parts, offering a complete mobile entertainment package," said Devinder Kishore, Director (Marketing), Nokia India. Combined with landscape gaming and dedicated gaming keys for additional comfort, the Nokia N85 breaks the boundaries of mobile gameplay."

In addition to games, the Nokia N85 comes with a strong lineup of multimedia features. It offers an in-built FM transmitter, 5 megapixel camera with Carl Zeiss optics and location tagging capabilities, a three month integrated license for turn-by-turn voice navigation and high-speed connectivity.

Heading: Rail budget hotel hits a roadblock, yet again - Indian Express
Content:
Rated at number four at the moment, India would be world's second largest economy by 2050 after China. While India will take Japan, China will edge out USA.

J Sadakkudulla, Regional Director, Reserve Bank of India, stated this while delivering a keynote address at the 5th International Conference on "Indian Capital Market - The Way Ahead", organised jointly by Punjabi University's Punjab School of Management Studies and Punjab Commerce and Management Association on Sunday.

Sadakkudulla said that while the continuing worsening global financial market has virtually crippled the world economy, India has been able to weather the storm to a great extent only due its time-tested conservative and semi-closed economic principles.

Referring to the slump in the Indian stock markets, Sadakkudulla said that the index revolving round 10,000 was optimum for the Indian economy as higher value than this was "good only for the greedy and not for the needy."

The Reserve Bank and the Indian Government, he said, were all set to take pre-emptive measures to contain excess volatility and alleviate the recent transient pressures on the domestic financial markets to increase capital inflows to improve liquidity conditions to ensure domestic financial stability.

Jaspal Singh, Vice-Chancellor, said that the turmoil in global financial market has put a question mark on the wisdom of the predictors of financial world.

Elaborating the concept, he said while the investors have to live with some degree of volatility, the Indian financial managers have to upgrade the risk management system and strengthen the regulatory frameworks to save the small investors from the shock treatment.

Conference Coordinator, Pushpinder Gill said that we need to explore possibilities of reforming the international financial structure in order to stabilise the global economic meltdown as business was all about to manage change in technology, markets, corporate cultures and global environment.

Sunil Gupta, Vice-Chancellor of Himachal Pradesh University, Shimla, was presented PCMA Lifetime Achievement Award by the V-C on the occasion.

Heading: City sees light: on health grounds, fruits on gift list - Indian Express
Content:
Three years after the Railway's mooted the proposal for a Budget Hotel near the Chandigarh Railway Station, the project hangs fire. While the Expression of Interest (EoI) for the hotel was received by the interested parties three years ago, construction for the same has not taken off till today.

The Indian Railway Catering and Tourism Corporation Ltd (IRCTC), the nodal agency for the project, failed to initiate the construction work despite the fact that the tender for the same was finalised in 2007 and the project was licensed to Zoom Developers, a Mumbai-based company.

"The project has not been able to take off as tenders for rates will be invited again at revised rates. As the rates of steel and cement have increased manifold in last few months, it is required to renegotiate the rates through financial bids with shortlisted company," said Aneet Dulat Chief Regional Manager, IRCTC.

This is not the first time that the project hit a roadblock. Earlier, the project when interested parties wanted a guarantee from the land provider to ensure that the terms of land use do not change mid-way.

The Budget Hotel is proposed to have four floors, a food court and 60 rooms. The entire process of booking rooms will be done through Internet and rented out at controlled prices. Apart from food and lodging, services like cabs and taxis will also be provided to the visitors.

Heading: On spat with DC, BJP leader says ‘We have patched up’ - Indian Express
Content:
Keeping in view the health hazards, the city has turned health conscious. Unlike previous years, the fad has changed from dry fruits and sweets to fruits and juices.

Vikram, a fruit seller, said, "People are buying apples and other juicy fruits in bulk as a gift item. Dates and juices are equally popular. This time I am doing good business."

Punjab State Fruit and Vegetable Commission Agents Association General Secretary Amardeep Singh said, "People prefer fruits and juices to other eatables. Courtesy the awareness regarding healthy eating that people have switched over to fruits and juices."

Dr Kuldeep Singh, a doctor, said, "It is good to eat fresh fruits and dry fruits. Fruits have minerals and dry fruits provide good cholesterol to the body. Though high in calories, nuts are also high in fibre and protect the heart in many ways. The protein in nuts is high in agrinine — an amino acid that relaxes blood vessels and increases blood flow. But sweets should be consumed less as these contain saturated fat which is not good for health."

Moreover, recent news of seizing the spurious "khoa" has alerted people. Jagvinder Singh, a serviceman, said, "Prevention is better than cure. We have decided not to eat sweets."

City roads become orderly

This city finds the much needed semblance of order only during VIP visits. The traffic in the city, which had over the last few days gone for a toss, was in a perfect order today - thanks to the chief minister, who was on his Sangat Darshan spree today.

Though traffic woes ended for sometime, yet, the security in place for the chief minister irked residents. And true to his style, the Chief Minister has asked city SSP R K Jaiswal to ensure that such things do not happen again.

The SSP added, "There is no other way out. Such things happen, but, then the security of the chief minister is our priority."

The otherwise thin number of policemen manning traffic on regular days swelled to a reasonable number today morning ahead of Badal's visit to the city.

Badal was supposed to meet the public at the Pindi Dayal Dharamshala, Chanan Devi Government High School in Salem Tabri, SAN Jain School Daresi, Sekhewal. The chief minister's cavalcade passed through the narrow streets of the old city area which is otherwise difficult to negotiate with on ordinary days.

Ramesh Singla, a businessman, quipped, "This is a very congested area where traffic jams are a regular feature but today the scene was totally pleasant. With traffic police manning the traffic, moving on these roads is so easy. We hope they maintain this practice and not disband it once the CM leaves the city."

Heading: Two-year PAUTA term was being grossly misused: Mahal - Indian Express
Content:
The acrimony surrounding the relation between BJP leader Sat Pal Gosain and Deputy Commissioner Sumer Singh Gurjar appears to have cooled down after the intervention of "some common friends and well wishers", claims the BJP leader.

Gosain has been instrumental in lodging a list of complaints with Chief Minister Parkash Singh Badal against the DC, to the extent of even demanding an inquiry by the Vigilance Bureau.

While speaking with Newsline, Gosain said, "We have patched up now. Some common friends helped us to do that and now I have nothing against the DC."

On the VB inquiry, the BJP leader said, "Though I do not want any inquiry as of now, I will still keep an eye on the working of the DC and if he starts troubling the general public again, I will restart my opposition."

Interestingly though, even while talking of compromise, Gosain was full of complaints against the DC.

"I had been getting lots of complaints against the DC. People came to me with proofs that he accepted petty bribes to do their work.

The DC refused to give a No-Objection Certificate (NOC) for a petrol pump to a person known to me despite the fact that he fulfilled all the formalities," said the BJP leader.

He added, "Also, we all know that the stalls for selling crackers were allocated to people who had little to do with the business."

Gosain further added, "The very people who got these stalls allocated in their name illegally sold these stalls to other people. All this is wrong and needed to be taken up."

While Deputy Commissioner Sumer Singh

Gurjar was not available for his comments, a senior Akali leader said, "All this mudslinging business in public, aimed at the Head of the district, was in a bad taste.

If some MLA had a problem, he should have sorted it out amicably instead of adopting this attitude.

The Akali leader added, "Everybody knows how the allocation of cracker stalls was done. Those who did not get them were bound to raise this hue and cry. Fortunately, the matter is now resolved."

Heading: This former national-level footballer tackles a life in penury - Indian Express
Content:
The victory of his group in the Punjab Agricultural University Teachers' Association (PAUTA) elections was a major surprise as he took on the established PAUTA regime on the campus. All through his tenure, Dr M S Mahal, president, PAUTA, faced the allegations of being a non-doer but his victory for the second term has silenced his detractors. Amrita Chaudhry catches up with Dr Mahal to find out what helped his team sweep the recent PAUTA elections.

Q You won the elections last year as teachers wanted a change. What was your strategy this time?

While in power, we have been open, honest and clear. It may sound clichéd but it is true. Irrespective of group alliances, we worked for the welfare of the teaching faculty. We always maintained that we need not adopt a confrontationist attitude just for the heck of it, when argument and talks across the table can get your work done. We did take a stand where it was needed yet on the whole, we never tried to oppose the administration just because we were supposed to. This in turn was our winning point. The faculty knew that we were a successful team and hence they elected us again.

Q Your team reduced the PAUTA term from two years to one. Do you think that one year was enough to get the work done?

Our idea was that when you know you are in power for a year, you will always be on your toes. We feel the two-year term was being grossly misused.

Q But then your team has drawn the flak for not sending correct reports to the Pay Commission or handing over the faculty guest house to non-teaching club?

Getting the new pay scale implemented in the true spirit is our priority and we will do that. As far as the issue of the non-teaching staff getting a part of our guest house to set up their club is concerned, we should not forget that the faculty club was supposed to be for both teachers and non-teachers. The guest house arrangement is temporary for the space is too small for a club. The non-teachers will, sooner or later, have to shift to a larger space.

We should not forget that non-teachers, Class IV employees, students and teachers are the four wheels on which the university runs. We all have to work together in tandem to get the desired results.

Q What are you priorities?

Our main issue is to get the new pay commission implemented. Maintaining the distinct identity of the agriculture scientists is another issue we want to work on. We, at PAU, are different from scientists of traditional universities. Our work entails field work, three increments for our masters rather than two and other such issues. In short, the UGC should recognise the fact that the agriculture scientists have to be treated differently from the scientists from the traditional universities.

Heading: Road to perdition: Medical negligence behind roadside deliveries in Gujarat - Indian Express
Content:
Had he imagined that he would have to face tough financial times in the later years of his life, former national-level football player Jagjit Singh would have gained higher education, which would have helped him get a secure future.

But, as luck was not on his side, the player, once excellent in netting the football into the goalpost, is now finding it hard to achieve the real goal of life — making both ends meet.

Jagjit Singh, who once represented the Punjabi University in many inter-university football tournaments, is now working at a cloth shop in the Field Ganj area as a salesman drawing Rs 2,500 a month.

A majority of his income goes into paying the rent of the house where he lives with his family. His family comprises his wife, a daughter and two sons. They stay in a small rented house in Field Ganj as they had to sell off their own big house due to the illness of Jagjit Singh.

Jagjit Singh, who once worked as a sub-inspector with the Cooperative Department of the Punjab government, had to leave his job in 1985 after he developed fistula on his hip.

"The next 13 years have been a long nightmare. Not only was I unable to sit and sleep, but also we had to sell off our properties for bearing the cost of my treatment.

During these years, I underwent surgeries seven times at reputed hospitals, not only in the city, but also at Chandigarh and Delhi. Finally, I was cured by a local doctor about four years ago," Jagjit Singh told Newsline.

As if it was not enough, after recovering from the fistula, he went into depression for about three years. "After coming out of depression, I started my life afresh and had to take up this petty job," he said.

But it is not his bad financial condition which perturbs Jagjit Singh.

More than his financial condition, it is the discontinuation of studies of his children that perturbs him. While his daughter Sandeep Kaur (20) and elder son Tejinder Singh (18) managed to study till Class XII, his younger son Prabhjot Singh (16) was not that lucky. He had to stop studies after Class X.

"My sons have taken up small private jobs for meagre salaries to share my burden. I wanted them to pursue higher studies and get good jobs," sobbed Jagjit Singh.

Jagjit Singh's wife Paramjit Kaur, who also was once a district-level player of basketball, also does her bit by doing embroidery work. "But that work hardly fetches us a decent income," she added .

He said that he feels sad that while the government has failed to provide him any help in his adverse years.

Heading: Life sentence after a lifetime of litigation - Indian Express
Content:
Even with the government's Chiranjeevi Yojana in place, there has been no decline in the number of roadside deliveries in villages and tribal areas of central Gujarat.

While majority of the cases happen due to the unavailability of medical staff at the Primary Health Centres (PHC) and Community Health Centres (CHC) from where they are sent to other nearby hospitals, many roadside deliveries happen due to incorrect due dates predicted by PHC officials.

There are over 16 CHCs, 76 PHCs and 465 Sub Centres (SCs) among 12 talukas of Vadodara district; but the medical facilities available to the villages are far from what it is on paper.

Village records and NGOs working in the rural areas have recorded over 20 roadside deliveries in Savli, Sankheda and Dabhoi between April and September this year, while more such cases are predicted in the tribal belt.

"Over 60 per cent of the posts at the SCs, PHCs and CHCs are vacant till date in Sankheda. While the PHCs are not competent enough to handle delivery cases, the CHCs too refuse to take cases with complications. Where on an average a CHC should have at least 25-30 delivery cases in a month, many centres have only 7-8 cases that are normal," said a medical official in Sankheda on condition of anonymity.

Most expecting mothers in the rural belt undergo complications like convulsion and sepsis, as most patients suffer from anaemia, lack of immunisation, malnutrition and other prenatal problems. "Most of the Sub Centres in the villages are either in a dilapidated condition or quite far off. The nurses visit the centres once in many months because of which the women in the village are neither properly monitored nor do they get medicines. Many times the emergency services reach hours after we call, which lead to deliveries on the way," said Urmila Panchal, a resident of Bodlav village in Sankheda.

Another villager, Jyoti Parmar, expressing her ire, said: "You won't believe but the nurses refuse to give BCG vaccines to infants, as they think the entire set would go waste if they open it for one child. And before there are a few more infants in the village, the first one is already over a month old."

The officials, however, dismiss the fact about roadside deliveries and other loopholes. "There is a level of negligence in the PHCs and CHCs. The doctors and nurses often misjudge the due date because of which deliveries happen much before the estimated time. The CHCs also lack gynaecologists because of which the patients have to be sent to other centres or general hospitals," said Dr. KR Soni, Block Health Officer (BHO), Dabhoi.

The Chief District Health Officer (CDHO), Dr. Itare Bhagwati, holds a different opinion. "I completely disagree with this. Our survey data speaks of a competent medical system. The tribal zones do face such problems but in the peripheral villages, the medical system has no problem," he said.

Heading: Meltdown effect: Banks have already started feeling the heat - Indian Express
Content:
Sessions court sentences four former employees of Lubi Electrical Ltd accused of killing a youth in 1987

The Ahmedabad City Civil and Sessions Court has sentenced four former employees of Lubi Electrical Limited to life imprisonment in a 21-year-old case.

The court also came down heavily on the investigating officers in the case for the delay and the shoddy nature of investigation. The verdict in the case came on Friday, after more than two decades of litigation.

Jagdish Thakar, Mukesh Thakur, Raju Madrasi and Mahipal Singh were sentenced for life for the murder of one Manu Singh, who was killed in a firing carried out by the accused to dispel a crowd of agitating workers. All the four had been out on bail for the last 18 years.

The incident had occurred in 1987, when a group of workers of the company had been protesting against the non-payment of minimum wages. In the firing incident, apart from the death of Manu Singh, who happened to be an innocent passerby, 18 other workmen had been injured.

The Sessions Court has also directed the convicts to pay a compensation of Rs 3 lakh to the wife of Manu Singh and Rs 25,000 each to the three workers who were injured and had testified before the court.

The court also passed strictures against the police and observed that "there was a deliberate attempt to save the accused" on their part. It has also ordered action against the police officers involved in shielding the accused.

Meanwhile, in another related case of payment of minimum wages, Lubi Electricals Limited, which employs about 1600 people, lost the case before a single-judge bench of the Gujarat High Court. The company has now appealed before a division bench of the High Court where the matter is still pending.

Heading: Textile industry has turned into a sunrise industry, says Vaghela - Indian Express
Content:
Credit-deposit ratio plummets below 40 per cent in six districts of Gujarat

With the credit-deposit ratio (CDR) of the banks (both public and private sector) having fallen in the state in the first quarter of the current financial year, banking experts say it is an indicator of the economic slowdown.

Following this development, bank authorities in Gujarat have also issued instructions to banks with CDR below 40 per cent to put in special efforts to boost the economy. Banks in the six districts of Anand, Dangs, Kheda, Kutch, Navsari and Porbandar have reported a CDR below 40 per cent.

According to the figures available, CDR of the banks in Gujarat decreased by an average of 3.15 per cent in the quarter that ended in June 2008. The private and District Central Cooperative Banks (DCCB) have been witnessing a maximum decrease of 7.5 per cent. However, the overall increase in deposits in all the banks has been an average five per cent with private banks showing a deposit growth of over eight per cent. In absolute terms, the deposits in Gujarat grew from Rs 1, 54,832 crore in March 2008 to Rs 1, 62,599 crore in June 2008, registering a growth of five per cent against 3.97 per cent during the corresponding period in the previous year.

However, the overall growth in advances in the state had an average of just one per cent, with private banks registering a growth in outstanding advances by less than two per cent. In fact, the growth in credit expansion by DCCBs and Gujarat State Cooperative Agricultural and Rural Development Bank (GSCARDB) registered a negative trend when the quarter ended in June 2008. Even lending to priority sectors by all banks registered a negative growth in the state.

Commenting on the falling CDR and negative growth trends in lending in the state in the last few months, finance and investment expert Mahendrasinh Solanki said that it was the sluggish economic environment that affected the overall bank performance, particularly towards advancement of loans, owing to overall global slowdown.

Vice-president of the Gujarat Chamber of Commerce and Industry (GCCI) Biren Parekh agreed that it was the economic slowdown that has adversely affected investment in Gujarat. However, he said that this phase would not last long with the Union government taking steps to reduce bank lending rates.

Heading: Witch hunting: Police accused of harassing ‘usual suspects’ - Indian Express
Content:
Thanks to the rationalisation of duty structure and government policies over the last four years, the textile industry has again turned into a sunrise industry from a sunset industry, said Union Textile Minister Shankersinh Vaghela here on Sunday.

Speaking to reporters, he said the country's cotton situation was comfortable enough to enable farmers get better prices, provided they exercised patience and waited for some more time before selling their produce.

The minister said that this year, there was a jump of 38 to 40 per cent in the minimum support price (MSP) of cotton set by the Cotton Corporation of India (CCI) compared to the previous year. He said the cotton output had gone up this year and the textile sector had seen investments flowing in for the last four years.

Pointing out that the MSP for cotton had increased to Rs 970 per quintal for 2008-09, Vaghela said the higher MSP would ensure maximum returns to the farmers.

According to the figures released by the Textile Ministry, between 2004 and 2008, the investment in the textile sector has been Rs 1.05 lakh crore and it is expected to touch Rs 1.5 lakh crore by 2012. The enhanced investment is estimated to generate 17.37 million jobs by 2012.

Cotton production, he said, was estimated to be 320 lakh bales (170 kg each) of which 100 lakh bales would be for export. Quoting 'Technology Mission on Cotton', he said that yield of cotton, especially in Gujarat, had registered 760 kg per hectare and 600 kg per hectare elsewhere . It was 400 kg per hectare in 2004.

Heading: Parliamentary panel to Home Ministry: Plug ‘porous points’ in Sir Creek area - Indian Express
Content:
Court had given them a clean chit in the 2002 blast case, the three now, accuse cops of troubling them after the Modasa incident

Three accused in the 2002 Panchmahals bomb blast case have written a letter to the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), seeking its intervention in alleged harassment by state police officials.

The copies of the letter have also been sent to Chief Minister Narendra Modi and state Home Minister Amit Shah.

The three — Sadiq Sindhi, Mohammed Yousuf Giteli and Elias Ubali — were accused of planting bombs in Polan Bazaar in Godhra, in a bus at Lunawada, Delol and Balasinor in July 2002. However, Panchmahals District Court had later released them, as the local Crime Branch that was investigating the case could not provide any evidence.

Now, after six years, Sindhi has stated in the letter that the three had been summoned in connection with the Ahmedabad and Modasa bomb blasts.

Sindhi and others have also stated in the letter that after the Modasa blast, the police called them and made them wait for a whole day.

"The next day, we got a call from the Godhra Town Police Station and we were being told that we have to go to Ahmedabad. Like before, we cooperated. But later, we were taken to Himmatnagar and then to Modasa, blindfolded," said Sindhi and others in the letter.

Sindhi then goes on to question the right of the police to blindfold him and his friends when they had been set free by the court.

A Godhra-based businessman, Sadiq used to work in the relief camps set up right after the post-Godhra carnage riots.

"The reasons could be many. We vehemently opposed the police's version of the story about the Godhra carnage. Those policemen, who had been investigating the matter, had a lopsided view about the incident. When like a free thinking person, you seek genuine answers, this is what happens to you," said Sadiq.

Earlier, Deputy Superintendent of Police R V Asari, who had summoned the three after the Modasa blast, said they were picked up for routine questioning, as they were earlier accused in the blast.

Interestingly, even during the course of investigation of the Polan Bazar blasts in 2002 in Godhra, police brought one person, Peeru Hakimji, who was arrested from Bulundshahr in Uttar Pradesh to his place saying that Sadiq gave shelter to the accused. "We have evidence that we did not know this person and he never stayed at my house," said Sadiq.

Heading: Modasa blast: Vaghela accuses Modi govt of lacking will, calls police useless - Indian Express
Content:
A Parliamentary panel has directed the Union Home Ministry to plug "porous points" in the disputed Sir Creek sector to prevent use of coastal routes for fomenting terrorism from across the Indo-Pak border.

A panel team that visited Bhuj sector said: "Pakistan has started showing added interest in this area and has got a good build up of its forces opposite the creek area. Due to dispute in the Sir Creek sector, a rogue action by Pakistan cannot be ruled out."

In its 37-page report on border fencing and floodlighting projects of Indo-Pak border, the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs said the area of Sir Creek is disputed due to different perceptions of the two countries.

It said though the international border runs along the mid-stream of Sir Creek, vigil is much easier for the Pakistani forces as the mainland on Pakistan side is comparatively closer to the Sir Creek.

The report, however, said that any major intrusion will be extremely difficult due to marshy land and presence of mangroves. It said an issue which came up for special mention when a sub-committee visited the Bhuj sector was the "most likely threat" of infiltration and smuggling through creeks.

"As the creeks are interconnected, once the enemy makes an entry to one of the major creeks, he can move into any of the creeks in small craft," the report said.

Heading: Health cover to envelop entire state by 2009 - Indian Express
Content:
Union Textiles Minister Shankersinh Vaghela on Sunday made a scathing attack on the state government, saying it was not willing to nab the real culprits behind the Modasa blast even though Congress MP from Sabarkantha, Madhusudan Mistry had pointed at the suspects.

Addressing a press conference at Circuit House Annexe here, he said the Gujarat Police proved itself "useless" and that it was so politicised, it acted only on the orders issued by the Chief Minister's Office. He said the police have not arrested the accused till date, whereas the Maharashtra Police performed their duty.

The minister said the blasts in Modasa and Malegaon last month pointed towards the involvement of Hindu suspects connected with saffron outfits. He said he suspected that the same set of people had a role in the Surat bomb plantings as well.

"This proves that terror knows no religion and that it was a matter of concern that so far it was only one sided trend of targeting one community for suspicion and questioning," he said.

Neither the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) nor anyone else should try to shield the culprits, he added.

On Sadhvi Pragya Singh, he said her links with the BJP had already been exposed and the truth would come out once the court decided the case.

Madhusudan Mistry, MP from Sabarkantha and a close aide of Vaghela, said he had warned the police in his constituency about the culprits, but they never acted on his information.

If at all they acted, they combed only one particular area and questioned unrelated people which scuttled the investigation.

A 15-year-old boy was killed in the bomb blast in the Suka Bazaar area of Modasa town on September 29. A bomb with timer device was placed on a motorcycle, which exploded in a minority-dominated area in the month of Ramzan, just two days before Eid.

Heading: System shutdown: Computer engineer gets 20-yr sentence - Indian Express
Content:
With 20 lakh beneficiaries, Gujarat to have highest number of BPL families under health insurance scheme

With over five lakh below poverty line (BPL) families in five districts set to get benefits under a Centre-aided health insurance scheme by December, the UPA Government has given a go-ahead to Gujarat to launch the scheme across the state.

Under its Rashtriya Swasthya Bima Yojana, the Centre will contribute 75 per cent of the total annual premium per BPL family, while the state government will pay the remaining 25 per cent of the premium. Accordingly, the Centre will soon allocate a fund of Rs 125 crore to the state to implement the scheme.

Gujarat Health Commissioner Amarjit Singh told Newsline on Saturday that Gujarat would be the first state in the country to provide health insurance cover to the highest number of BPL families — around 20 lakh — when it is fully implemented across the state by April 2009.

In fact, three other states — Punjab, Haryana and Rajasthan — where the scheme has already been launched, have together covered only about four lakh such families till now. This is less than the 5.56 beneficiaries covered under the pilot project in Bharuch, Dahod, Jamnagar, Kutch and Patan, Singh said.

The government has engaged private insurance company Cholamandalam to implement the scheme in these five districts. The company has already launched a drive to prepare and distribute smart cards among the BPL families with the logistical support being provided by the various state government departments like Health, Rural Development and Panchayat.

Since the scheme mainly covers BPL workers and their families engaged in

the unorganised sector, the Union Labour and Employment Ministry has signed an MoU with the Gujarat government for its implementation.

"While in Bharuch most of the BPL families have been provided with smart cards, its distribution in other four districts will be over by November. We expect the BPL families in Bharuch to start availing the medical facilities from mid November under the scheme," said the

Health Commissioner.

After successfully launching the project, the government has initiated the process of inviting bids from private insurance firms to implement the scheme in the remaining 21 districts of Gujarat. When bids are finalised in the next few days, a drive to prepare and distribute smart cards among the BPL families will be launched in these

districts.

Under the scheme, the total amount insured will be Rs 30,000 per family who will have to pay only Rs 30 per annum as registration/renewal fees. The beneficiaries will be able to seek medical treatment for different diseases through a network of hospitals being run by private practitioners, public trusts and the government.

The insurance company will empanel the eligible health service providers under the scheme. The hospitals thus empanelled will provide surgical as well as clinical health services to the beneficiaries as per the insurance package to be worked out by insurers.

Heading: Slowdown casts a shadow on IIM-A fest - Indian Express
Content:
Sentenced in nine separate cases, he would drug and loot unsuspecting bus passengers

A local court has sentenced one Nitin Rameshchandra Bhatt, a computer engineer, to 20 years of rigorous imprisonment after being found guilty in nine cases of looting bus passengers.

Nitin has been awarded a five-year imprisonment term in three cases, nine years in three others and six years for another three, public prosecutor Garish Bhatt said, adding that the sentences would not run concurrently. Nitin, a native of Surat, used to rob passengers travelling by the State Transport buses. He would befriend unsuspecting passengers and then would offer them tea laced with sedatives, to render them unconscious. Thereafter, he would decamp with their valuables and belongings, the police said.

He was arrested nearly 10 months ago from Rajkot Central Bus Depot when he was moving in a suspicious manner, said the police. Some mobile phones, sim cards, ATM cards and medicines used to mix in the tea were recovered from him.

Nitin had looted cash and other valuables worth over Rs 3 lakh from as many as 10 passengers before his arrest. He had not engaged any lawyer and fought his case on his own.

Heading: Budding managers to rack their brains at IIM-A Insight - Indian Express
Content:
Organisers had a tough time convincing corporates to participate

The Consumer Market Research Fest (Insight-2008) of the Indian Institute of Management, Ahmedabad (IIM-A) opened on Sunday with a mix of enthusiasm and expectations. This year, expectations have been low, as the market downturn seems to have caught on with one of the country's premier institutes.

Apparently, the event organisers have had a tough time convincing corporates to participate, while the steady list of participant companies has hit rough waters. Event Secretary Prateek Agrawal points out: "We had to try very hard this time to convince the participating companies. Many of them had been pleased with our earlier projects, yet they backed out this time. The market downturn has made them cut down costs for campus activities drastically. Participation has been seriously affected."

Anish Passi, Corporate Communications coordinator for the event observed: "There has been a decline in sponsorships this year. Even those companies that participated after a lot of deliberation did not do so like last year. We had to tell them about the benefits about how we could customise results for them and its effect. However, we have been able to secure an almost equal number of projects as compared to the last year when the market was on a high. This time, the companies have been more cautious.

Although the slowdown started with investment banks, companies in all sectors have been affected."

The footfall this year was lower than last year's 6,000.

Heading: Chaotic Nashik Phata chowk: 16-yr-old hurt, misses exams - Indian Express
Content:
For the first time, teams from other institutes have been allowed entry at the consumer research fest

The Indian Institute of Management, Ahmedabad (IIM-A) has for the first time opened up its doors for B-schools from across the country to participate in the 23rd Consumer Market Research Fest— Insight-2008.

Insight, which happens to be IIM-A's oldest fest, has attracted participants like IBS (ICFAI Business School) Hyderabad, TAPMI (T A Pai Management Institute) Manipal, Welingkar Institute of Management, Mumbai and city-based Mudra Institute of Communications among others.

Four teams from these institutes, two from outstation

B-schools along with six teams from IIM-A are handling 12 projects this year. In the fest, participating groups collect research data by way of experiential research methodology and specially designed games for people of varied profiles. The final report of the projects will be submitted by mid-December.

With a total of nine companies participating this year and 12 participant groups chosen from among 83 entries for 12 projects, the fest is close to the previous years' average of 13 projects.

Event Secretary Pratik Agarwal said: "This year, we have tried to give a broader marketing perspective in the fest, while a 'case contest' (preparing an integrated marketing campaign for dabbawalas), held 20 days ago, has been introduced for the first time. The fest will be followed by another one."

Amid a daylong entertainment of antakshari, treasure hunt, a series of talent hunts, tambola and other absorbing games for adults as well as kids, the specially designed research games kept the audience engaged. Games like 'Dart the city' designed for Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation (AMC)'s Riverfront Development Project drew a huge crowd.

Ibrahim Ulde, first-year student of TAPMI, was enthused at the 'excellent' audience response. "Apart from the great response our project (Kaya Skin Clinic) is seeing today, this has been a great first-hand experience about doing market research," Ulde said.

Heading: As traffic cops tighten grip, vehicle owners and drivers squirm - Indian Express
Content:
Two weeks back, Newsline had taken up the traffic mess issue with PCMC city engineer and traffic police...they did not act. PCMC chief says it is cops' job, DCP says he will decongest the chowk

At the chaotic Nashik Phata chowk in Pimpri-Chinchwad, 16-year-old Megha Kharatmal, a college student, survived a near fatal accident on Friday morning.

Megha was about to cross the Pune-Mumbai highway at the Nashik Phata chowk when a two-wheeler zoomed in from the blind corner from Bhosari side and ran into her. Megha suffered injuries on right hand, legs and on the head. A CT scan was also done to know whether she suffered any serious injury.

After being discharged from a private hospital, Megha is now recuperating at her home in Kasarwadi. While the accident has caused her physical trauma, Megha is also worried about her exam results as she had to miss out on two oral papers. "The accident occurred when I was heading to the college for my English oral test. On Saturday too, I had to miss Marathi orals," said Megha, a Class XI student of Modern College, Shivajinagar.

Her family has incurred an expenditure of over Rs 5,000 for her medical treatment which is likely to go up as she will remain under treatment for at least a month. "I can't move, sit or walk...The pain is all over," says Megha.

Like Megha, several citizens — two-wheeler riders and cyclists — have met with accidents at the perennially chaotic Nashik Phata chowk in the last ten months. Almost every alternate day, one accident occurs at this chowk. Over two weeks ago, Newsline had taken up the issue with PCMC city engineer Eknath Ugile, who promised to set things right. "I will personally visit the sight and do whatever is possible," Ugile had said.

But the situation still remains the same. The chowk continues to be as chaotic as ever. Barely two days ago, two garbage containers, which were placed at the blind corner in the chowk, were removed only after the municipal commissioner issued directions. A drainage chamber has not been aligned to the road because of which speeding vehicles bump into it and get tossed in the air. On the road to Bhosari, six-seaters are lined up throughout the day creating difficulties for smooth flow of traffic. On the opposite side, three-seaters are parked. Compounding the confusion is the fact that the entire chowk has become a parking lot with vehicles occupying every inch of the space.

In front of the Sagar Corner building, an array of vehicles are parked, many of them right on the public road leading to local residential societies. "These parked vehicles are creating a huge traffic mess," says Sanjay Shah, chairman of of Goyal Residency. Everyday, 5000 residents use this road.

When this reporter complained to the traffic police, they said pointblank: "Only when a photograph is published in the newspaper, our bosses will act."

PCMC executive engineer Madanmohan Savle said he will inspect the chowk and take necessary action on Monday. Municipal Commissioner Asheesh Sharma said, "It is the duty of the police to initiate appropriate action to help smooth flow of traffic." Deputy Commissioner of Police (Traffic) Manoj Patil said he has just transferred an officer from Nashik Phata and will try to decongest the chowk.

Heading: Safety concerns: Sassoon hospital deploys 90 more security guards - Indian Express
Content:
Strict measures introduced to control traffic during CYG are here to stay even after Diwali, says police

With a huge number of handcart vendors, jeep and bus drivers and autorickshaw owners reluctant to ply on the city roads fearing prosecution from the city police department, this Diwali is going to be a dark one, at least for over 30,000 rickshaw drivers and hand cart vendors in the city, said Maharashtra Kamgar Sabha president Nana Kshirsagar on the recent crackdown of the city police on various private vehicles in the city. Kshirsagar said, "They (the police) had asked us to shut shop during the CYG. They also said that as the area is very congested and crowded, it is a touted hotspot for planting bombs or disrupting traffic. Keeping in mind the importance of the game we complied with all their requests. In fact, all the hawkers and drivers of private vehicles ensured that they did not break any rules. However, the large number of private vehicles, rickshaws and handcart owners who have been prosecuted tell a different story. The police are just using their muscle power to increase the misery of the common man."

The city police had stepped up efforts to control unruly traffic on the road to the Commonwealth Youth Games venue. But, these efforts to bring civility to the traffic scenario have been met with sharp criticism, especially from owners of private vehicles and hawkers.

DCP Manoj Patil (Traffic) said, "The vehicles that have been picked up in the last one month were either illegally plying in the city or had legal permits but were found plying more people than allowed. The plan was intended not only for the CYG or Diwali, but from now on, the city police will crack down on vehicles illegally ferrying people. Those vehicles that have been taken in are detained under Section 207 of the Motor Vehicles Act." During the games, the amount of money collected in terms of fines is over Rs 35 lakh. Patil said, "We normally collect such a huge amount in a month. However, following strict procedures we ended up collecting this amount in a shorter period. This will continue and anyone found on the wrong side of the law will be dealt with severely." Kshirsagar said, "We, the common people, are the ones who are being put to task by everyone — the police top brass and bureaucrats.

No one is ready to sympathise with the cause of the common man. We have, therefore, decided to carry out an 'andholan' outside the Commissioner's office on Monday to put forth our demands."

Heading: Tiny tots put up thought-provoking show - Indian Express
Content:
After about a dozen cases of theft and attacks on the Sassoon General Hospital's doctors and nurses in the recent past, the hospital has now deployed 90 security guards in its premises. This was followed by the protests held by doctors demanding the deployment of more security personnel.

"These 90 guards, including stand-by staff, will work in three shifts," said Dr Nirmala Borade, acting dean of the hospital. Most of the security men are ex-servicemen. After the Department of Medical Education and Research (DMER) refused to provide security personnel, it was the Pune Zilla Suraksha Samiti, a government body, that has arranged for these guards, she added.

It was only last week that a patient's relatives, in a drunken state, abused a resident doctor on duty.

The Maharashtra Association of Resident Doctors had given the hospital authorities an ultimatum of October 22 to put the revised security system in place. There are nearly 300 resident doctors at Sassoon, apart from the 150-odd medical interns.

Heading: MNS corporator, five others arrested for vandalism - Indian Express
Content:
Global Indian International School (GIIS), a venture of the Goel Ganga Group, celebrated their second annual day at the Acharya Atre Auditorium at Sant Tukaramnagar on October 15, amidst much fanfare.

The special guests present on the occasion were the participating contingent of Guernsey, the country which the GIIS school was hosting as part of the 'Bond Forever' programme of the Commonwealth Youth Games. The team manager presented the school with their customary urn and brochures about the country. Sonu Gupta, director, GIIS, thanked the school for the initiative taken in hosting them and also for the gifts prepared by the children for them .

The pre-primary students of the school enthralled the audience with various presentations on the theme 'Glimpses of the Wild'. The school choir group chanted Sanskrit shlokas to mark the beginning of the event. The principal welcomed the guests and the dignitaries which included Chandu Borde, vice principal of Global Indian Foundation.

The tiny tots of the nursery enacted some rhymes and wooed the audience with foot tapping numbers. The students of Kindergarten I presented a Marathi play titled Pancharangi Khar. It was about the animal world that was colourless in the beginning and God blessing the world subsequently with colours. The squirrel was late when the 'colours' were being distributed by God but he too makes up for the lost time and is blessed with stripes on its body. The most delightful and enchanting presentation was by the students of Kindergarten II titled 'Zelda The Zebra'.

It was a dance presentation about a zebra who loses its stripes and the hunt thereafter in search of them. The enchanting costumes and their antics fascinated the audience.

Chief guest Vivek Aranha, chairman, Rosary Education Group, Pune, congratulated the teachers and the parents for working in cohesion for producing an event of this magnitude.

Heading: Thermax second quarter revenues up - Indian Express
Content:
The Kothrud police today arrested Maharashtra Navnirman Sena Corporator Rajendra Keshav Gorade, alias Rajabhau Gorade, for vandalism. The incident occured when MNS chief Raj Thackeray was arrested after north Indian students were beaten up by MNS members during the railway recruitment board exams recently.

Gorade was arrested along with five others — Nagesh Dhamale, Sushant Chapekar, Shridhar Khangre, Vaibhav Tagude and Dayanand Gaikwad.

The accused have been charged under sections 435, 427, 34 and 109 of the IPC. They were produced in the court on Sunday and have been sent to police custody for one day. They will be produced in court again on Monday.

Gorade and his men were involved in the destruction of public property including buses in Kothrud.

Heading: Show must go on - Indian Express
Content:
Thermax Limited, a leading player in energy and environment solutions, today announced its results for the second quarter of fiscal 2008-09.

Total operating income was Rs. 804.1 crore compared to Rs. 770.1 crore in the same quarter of the previous year. Net profit stood at Rs.57 crore compared to Rs. 69.2 crore in Q2 last year. The Q2 profit reported is after providing for foreign exchange losses of Rs.37.4 crore for the quarter (last year gain Rs. 3 crore). In the first half of the financial year the company's net profit stood at Rs. 120.7 crore (Rs.125.2 crore) and the total operating income was Rs. 1521 crore (Rs.1436.6 crore). The profit reported for the half year is after providing for foreign exchange losses of Rs. 53.1 crore (last year gain Rs. 7.2 crore).

Heading: Born free - Indian Express
Content:
As we celebrate during the much awaited festival of the year, there are a few for whom Diwali just means another working day

Diwali has started and the frenzy of cleaning, cooking, decorating, buying gifts, firecrackers is almost over. Celebration is all that's on the cards. While most of us prepare to kick back and relax with friends and families during the holidays, there are a few others, for whom these festive days are nothing but another week at work. It takes people from a cross section of occupations to ensure that while we revel in the festivities, society continues to function smoothly.

Divyanshu Boora is a 24-year-old software engineer working for a multinational company. "We monitor servers based across the globe. All software and services have problems. If everyone took leave the entire network could collapse, and not just in India," says Boora who will thus be working throughout Diwali "I am not too upset about working on Diwali; my family stays in Haryana so for me, the weekend will be more like Diwali," he grins.

Another section of the society that runs non-stop is the travel and tourism industry. Priyanka Sahani works for a private airline company. This will be her first working Diwali. "You cannot have flights on standstill for the whole day," she exclaims. The cabin crews, ground staff, cleaners, attendants, all have to work round the clock to keep the ball rolling. I do not have any big plans, but maybe I can take off early and spend at least the latter part of the evening with my family," she hopes fervently.

While for some it is their company policy, for others it is a question of survival. Nurruddin Mullick has come all the way from Kolkatta to find work here in Pune. He works as a two-wheeler parking lot attendant at the J J Garden parking lot off M G Road. "We do not even get weekly offs. I work for 12 hours everyday, with one day off a month. Diwali is in fact a season when the number of visitors to public places is high, turning parking lots into utter chaos if not supervised. This Diwali is definitely not a holiday for me as I am saving up to go home after six months," he says. He shares a room with his uncle and brother who also have come looking for work.

Rickshaw driver Balu Korpade, narrates a similar story. He has been traversing the city streets for the past 12 years. "It depends on us whether we want to take a break from work. Diwali day means more business, hence it is not practical to stay at home. I work from nine in the morning to nine at night, so I will take my wife and kids out somewhere the day after Diwali, he says, revealing how people from different social stratas have different priorities.

For yet others it's neither the company nor survival, at least not theirs, that keeps them at work even during festivals. Doctors, nurses, ward boys, anesthetists and others in the noble medical profession have to put patients before themselves. Even if it's an official holiday, they often have to rush to hospital when emergencies arise.

Traffic Police officer U G Kadam sums days like these up in one sentence. "Job comes first," he emphasizes. "We usually get an off during the week so if we are lucky it may fall on Diwali, but these are unstable times. Especially taking into consideration the terrorist scares and other similar issues. I do miss spending time with my family, but things like this go with the job," he smiles.

A telling statement indeed, and a gentle reminder that while you paint the town red, somebody is watching your back. Diwali may be a stress buster and a sweet escape for society at large, but for these hardworking individuals, the show must go on.

Heading: Culinary vision - Indian Express
Content:
The Rajiv Gandhi Zoological Parks is getting a makeover. The aim is to provide a better habitat to animals and an eco-friendly environment to visitors

They are not criminals but in a caged environment they sure do seem to be serving an undeserved life sentence. Recognising this, the authorities of Rajiv Gandhi Zoological Park are in the process of changing mindsets. Slowly but steadily they are effecting a change in focus from treating animals as objects of observation to living beings that have the right to demand and get better living conditions.

As a part of providing natural habitat for animals, four new species of animals that include black buck, chinkara, jackal and wolf will very soon be shifted in naturalistic, moated enclosures in the park. "We have been functional since 1999 when the animals kept in cages in Peshwe Park were shifted to the current location in Katraj. At that time we had two monkey enclosures and two bear enclosures. Over the years, however, we worked on providing better habitat for the animals and now we are very soon planning to provide similar environment to four other species," says Kazveen Umrigar, director, Rajiv Gandhi Zoological Park.

The park, spread over 165 acres is a home for over 300 animals that include nearly 17 species of mammals, three species of birds and 24 species of reptiles. The authorities are also planning to take additional preventive measures to ensure a clean and pollution free environment both for visitors as well as for the animals. "We have banned plastic bags inside the premises. Also we have recently introduced two battery-operated vehicles that will take the visitors through the park," says Umrigar. "Very soon we are also planning to undertake the renovation work of the snake park section. Currently the snakes are kept in pits and that is not an ideal condition for the snakes to survive. We will be providing ideal living conditions for these reptiles as well," adds she.

A recently undertaken venture also includes a vulture conservation programme under which the endangered species of vultures called- Long Billed vultures are protected and taken care of. "These are big black birds with long neck and bald head. Though noisy eaters, these birds play a major role in keeping the environment clean. Given a rapid decline in their population, they now fall in the category of endangered species. Their percentage has come down by 97 per cent," she adds.

With over half of the zoo already renovated and open for visitors, the changes have not only acted as a relief for animals but have also increased the number of visitors. "Today, they can see animals in their natural forms; for instance, a tiger sharpening its claws, monkey and birds on the trees and so on. In fact the number of visitors has gone up to as high as 15,000 visitors a day on holidays and there are many who come and appreciate the new look of the park," says Umrigar.

Heading: Spin Out: ICS college winners, IBMR the runners-up - Indian Express
Content:
With special kitchen for visually-challenged, life might just become a bit easier for them

They can win the world when it comes to academics or art, but the painful moment for a visually impaired mother is that when her child demands a homemade dish and she finds herself dependant on somebody else. However, needs begets invention, and here is a kitchen that's made to bring smile on a child face and content to a visually challenged mother.

After Louis Braille invented the unique writing for visually impaired in 1821, life had become much more than a dark world for them. However, with time, grew the expectation and after achieving in the campus, they also want to experience the joys of taking care of all their needs themselves- be it housekeeping or cooking.

While kitchen was always considered not-so-safe place for them, Concepts, an interior solution business and Amar Rane, a celebrity chef, have come together to make kitchen for visually challenged a reality. Rane has been running a cookery course for visually challenged but their students did face a problem in experimenting the recipes in the kitchen without aid. From there came the idea of kitchen for visually impaired. Rane is the official brand ambassador of Concepts.

"Visually challenged girls are no different from other girls, who want to cook and win appreciation from their family members. And despite knowing the recipes, they have to depend on others to cook, which again involves danger given the fire and sharp objects in the kitchen. When I came to know about this kitchen for visually challenged, I couldn't stop myself from associating with it, as this gives me another opportunity to help visually impaired people," says Rane, who explained the nitty-gritty of cooking so that a model kitchen could be developed.

While the jars would have stickers on which name of content would be written in Braille, the drawers would also have aluminum labels that will read the types of content that drawer has. Also they have pasted signs that can be sensed by touching.

"We have put three button-like signs in front of the gas burner to suggest that that is the high pressure burner and two signs for a medium pressure burner and so on. Similar signs are put on the drawers to suggest the size of container, three signs for bigger vessel and one for smaller," explains Rane.

Mandar Vilas Thakur, partner, Concepts, says, "Apart from the signs we are also developing sinks and chopping board in the drawer itself. This is done for physically challenged persons who work on wheelchairs. They can pull the drawer that come with adjustable level and do the cutting and grating there. Even the electric points are placed within their reach in the kitchen that we would develop."

Heading: Special shows for festive season - Indian Express
Content:
A two-day event called Spin Out 2008 was organised by IBMR on October 11 and 13 at IBMR (Institute of Business management and research) Campus at Chinchwad. Spin Out 2008 is the initiative taken by first year students of MCA and MCM with participants from ICS, IIBR, CSIT & IBMR the colleges under ASM Group of Institutes.

Spin Out is an inter-collegiate information technology quiz competition wherein teams from various colleges (from ASM Group) participate. The two-day event turned out as a rich experience for computer students as an organiser as well as participant.

Spin out 2008 was mainly driven by students of ASM institute to avail of exposure to the new trends of the IT world.

ICS college emerged as a winner followed by IBMR who bagged the runners -up trophy.

Prof J A Kulkarni was the chief guest of the Spin Out 2008 award ceremony. During his speech after distributing the prizes, he emphasised the need for extracurricular activity along with academic sessions.

Prof J.K.Lahir while welcoming the chief guest expressed his happiness that ASM students were progressing well in their pursuit of overall development.

Dr Sandeep Pachpande expressed his desire to lift the Spin Out event up national level and he expressed confidence in the way this event has generated awareness in the students.

Prof Chandrakant Thakare and Prof Pallavi Thorat were the co-ordinators of the event.

Heading: Bharat Forge surges ahead - Indian Express

Heading: Small talk - Indian Express
Content:
Bharat Forge, the flagship company of Kalyani Group and a leading global supplier of forged and machined components recently announced its second quarter results with combined revenue reaching Rs 1,360 crore and PBT (before exceptional items) of Rs 117 crore, a growth of 28 and 8 per cent respectively.
